docs.title: cctrace
docs.text:
Self-hosted telemetry for Claude Code and Codex CLI sessions.

cctrace collects what your coding-agent sessions did — token usage, cost, tool calls, and the conversation itself — into a database you run, and serves a dashboard over it. The agent's OpenTelemetry output answers "how much", the session transcripts answer "what happened"; cctrace ingests both and keeps them joined per session.

How cctrace collects coding-agent sessions On each developer machine, Claude Code sends OTLP over gRPC port 4317 and Codex CLI sends OTLP over HTTP port 4318 to cctraced. The cctrace sync daemon reads both agents' session JSONL files and uploads them to HTTP /api/sync on port 8080. In the server Docker Compose boundary, cctraced queues OTLP data through PGMQ, stores telemetry and session records in TimescaleDB, and serves an embedded Next.js static dashboard on port 8080, whose default host bind is 127.0.0.1. How cctrace collects coding-agent sessions Two ingestion paths, one self-hosted store OTLP/gRPC · TCP 4317 OTLP/HTTP · TCP 4318 HTTP /api/sync OTLP queue session rows Claude Code OTLP + JSONL Codex CLI OTLP + JSONL Session JSONL Claude + Codex cctrace sync daemon cctraced OTLP receivers REST API · /api/sync embedded web server 4317 · 4318 · 8080 Dashboard Next.js static export served by cctraced default bind 127.0.0.1:8080 TimescaleDB + PGMQ OTLP queues · telemetry and session tables DEVELOPER MACHINE SERVER · DOCKER COMPOSE

The dashboard above is a fictitious five-person team on a demo server, not a real deployment. See Dashboard pages for a page-by-page tour.

docs.title: How data gets in
docs.text:
Two ingestion paths feed one store, because neither is sufficient alone.

Path Source Transport Carries Latency OTEL the agent's OTLP exporter gRPC 4317 (Claude Code), HTTP 4318 (Codex) token counts, cost, metrics live Sync session JSONL files on disk HTTP /api/sync (port 8080) full conversation, tool calls periodic

cctrace init configures both on a developer machine: it points the agent's OTLP exporter at the server and registers the hooks that start the sync daemon.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Component Runs on Role cctrace each developer machine Client CLI and sync daemon. Watches the agent's session directory and uploads records. cctraced the server host Server. Receives OTLP, accepts sync uploads, serves the API and the dashboard. TimescaleDB + dashboard the server host Storage with compression and retention policies; the Next.js dashboard is embedded in cctraced.

The server and the database run as two containers from deploy/docker-compose.yml. Both images are built from this repository; neither is published to a registry.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not send telemetry to a third party. Besides the server you configure, the client queries Anthropic's usage API with the local Claude Code login to read plan limits, and the server downloads OpenAI's public pricing pages. See Privacy. The weekly AI report can send data to an outside AI provider once an admin enables it; it is under active development and not documented here.
  • It does not come as a hosted service or pre-built binaries. You build the client and the server images from source.
  • By default, clients built from this repository do not update themselves. The build links an empty update public key, so the client refuses automatic updates; you rebuild to upgrade. A server image signed with your own keys serves clients that do update themselves; see Security operations.
  • Clients built from this repository without an update or policy public key do not apply server policies either. A policy that moves clients to new server addresses is verified with those keys, so a client built with your own key applies it. See Sync daemon, and Security operations for signing one.

The dashboard stores conversation content. Decide retention and redaction before you connect a team: see Privacy.

Status

cctrace is early. The server API and the database schema still change between releases. Pin a version if you depend on either.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Getting started — run the server and connect one machine, end to end.
  • Server install — build the images, set the required values, start the stack.
  • Client install — build cctrace and put it on your PATH.
  • Reference — commands, server environment, ports, privacy settings.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Run the server and connect one machine to it, end to end. Everything below happens on a single machine that runs both the server stack and Claude Code, so every address is loopback (127.0.0.1).

Getting started: operator and developer steps The operator builds the two images, writes deploy/.env and starts the stack with docker compose up -d. The first admin created at /setup has no team, so the operator then adds a user account with a Team and a cctrace User ID, and hands the server URL and that account to the developer. The developer, who has built the client with make build-client, runs cctrace init, restarts the agent and checks cctrace status and the dashboard. OPERATOR DEVELOPER server URL + user account Build images docker build Configure deploy/.env Start stack compose up -d Create users /setup admin user + team + ID Build client make build-client Initialize cctrace init Restart the agent Verify cctrace status

Each step is the short path. The linked pages carry the full options and the reasons behind them.

docs.title: 1. Check the requirements
docs.text:
• Go 1.26 or later, to build the client.
  • Docker with Compose, to build and run the server and the database.
  • A clone of this repository. Run every command below from its root.

The server image builds the dashboard inside Docker, so this path does not need Node.js on the host.

docs.title: 2. Build the server images
docs.text:
Both image tags exist only locally; compose uses pull_policy: never and fails instead of pulling.

docker build -t cctrace/timescaledb-pgmq:latest docker/timescaledb-pgmq/
docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile --build-arg UPDATE_SIGNING=optional \
  -t cctrace/cctraced:latest .

UPDATE_SIGNING=optional builds without an update-signing key. Details: Server install.

docs.title: 3. Set the required values
docs.text:
Copy the example env file, then edit 3 keys: JWT_SECRET and LOGS_DIR have no default and the stack does not start without them; DB_PASSWORD ships with a placeholder you should not keep.

$ cp deploy/.env.example deploy/.env
$ jwt_secret=$(openssl rand -hex 32) && sed -i.bak "s|^JWT_SECRET=.*|JWT_SECRET=${jwt_secret}|" deploy/.env
$ db_password=$(openssl rand -hex 20) && sed -i.bak "s|^DB_PASSWORD=.*|DB_PASSWORD=${db_password}|" deploy/.env
$ LOGS_DIR=/absolute/path/on/the/host/for/logs && mkdir -p "$LOGS_DIR" && sed -i.bak "s|^LOGS_DIR=.*|LOGS_DIR=${LOGS_DIR}|" deploy/.env
$ rm deploy/.env.bak

Decide DB_PASSWORD before the first start

Postgres applies the password only when the data volume is initialised. Changing it later leaves the role on the old value, and cctraced restart-loops with password authentication failed. Recovering means dropping the database volume, which discards collected data.

deploy/.env.example lists every other value. The dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1:8080 by default; OTLP binds to all host interfaces on 4317 and 4318 without TLS. See Configuration before exposing the host to a network you do not control.

docs.title: 4. Start the stack
docs.text:
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml ps
$ curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/health

A bad value fails at server startup, not at up -d. If cctraced is restarting rather than Up, read its logs:

$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml logs cctraced

docs.title: 5. Create the first admin
docs.text:
1. Find the setup token in the same logs, on the line [cctraced] initial administrator setup token:. To choose the token yourself, set CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN in the .env file before the first start.

  2. Open http://127.0.0.1:8080. With no users yet, the dashboard sends you to /setup.

  3. Enter the setup token, your email, name, and a password of at least 8 characters.

The token stops working once the first admin exists. Details: First admin.

docs.title: 6. Create a user for the client
docs.text:
cctrace init signs in with a cctrace User ID, not an email, and refuses an account without a team. The first admin has neither. To connect as the admin, open its row menu on Users > Management, select Edit, and fill in Team and cctrace User ID. To connect as someone else, create a separate account:

  1. On Users > Management (/users), select Add User.

  2. Enter another email, a name, a Team, and a cctrace User ID such as alice. Keep the role user.

  3. Copy the temporary password the dialog shows.

  4. Sign out, sign in as the new account with the temporary password, and set a new password on the Settings page the dashboard sends you to.

cctrace init refuses the temporary password until it is changed. Details: Users.

docs.title: 7. Build and install the client
docs.text:
$ make build-client
$ sudo cp dist/cctrace /usr/local/bin/cctrace

make build-client builds for the current platform into the dist directory. If you skip the copy, cctrace init offers to install itself into /usr/local/bin (macOS and Linux) when it is not on your PATH.

Building needs Go. If your machine can instead reach the server over the network, download the matching binary from it and skip the Go toolchain entirely: see Client install.

docs.title: 8. Connect the client
docs.text:
$ cctrace init

Answer the prompts:

Prompt Value for this setup Sync endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8080 OTEL endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4317 User ID the cctrace User ID from step 6 Temporary password the new password you set in step 6 Enable session log sync? y

init writes the profile to ~/.cctrace/profile.json and applies the OTEL environment (gRPC to 4317) and the sync hooks to ~/.claude/settings.json. It then offers a read token for the analysis commands; collection does not need it, so you can answer n. If ~/.codex exists, it also offers Codex session sync and writes Codex's OTLP/HTTP exporter to port 4318 (see Codex CLI). Details: Connect.

docs.title: 9. Restart the agent
docs.text:
Restart Claude Code. Telemetry starts from the new process, and session log sync starts on its own from the next Claude Code session. Sessions from before the install are not backfilled. To sync without waiting, run:

$ cctrace sync

docs.title: 10. Confirm it works
docs.text:
$ cctrace status

Check the SERVER section for OTEL status: [OK] connected, and the PATHS section for Settings: ending in (applied). The command exits with status 2 when the OTEL endpoint is unreachable.

Then run a short Claude Code session and open http://127.0.0.1:8080/sessions. The session appears there once it has synced -- under the Interactive filter, which is the page's default, for an ordinary session with human turns. A machine-driven session (for example one started with claude -p) is a Headless session instead; switch to Headless or All to see it. See Dashboard pages.

If something does not show up, see Sync daemon and Operations.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text: cctrace collects Claude Code through two paths: OTEL telemetry that Claude Code sends to the server itself, and session logs that the sync daemon uploads. Both are configured in Claude Code's settings file.

docs.title: Where the settings go
docs.text:
cctrace init, cctrace env apply, cctrace profile add, and cctrace config set write into the settings file of the profile's Claude home: ~/.claude/settings.json for the default profile, or the directory a named profile points at. See Profiles.

The write keeps every key cctrace does not manage. Before writing, cctrace takes a snapshot and refuses to write if anything other than its own keys would change. It also refuses to overwrite a settings file that is not valid JSON. The file is replaced atomically and written with mode 0600.

docs.title: OTEL environment
docs.text:
These variables are set under env:

Variable Value CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY 1 OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER otlp OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER otlp OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ACCOUNT_UUID 1 OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL the profile's protocol, grpc by default; http/protobuf with a private CA (below) OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT the profile's OTEL endpoint; with a private CA, its OTLP/HTTP port (below) OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS Authorization=Bearer <upload token> OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL 60000 by default (options.metrics_export_interval) OTEL_LOGS_EXPORT_INTERVAL 5000 by default (options.logs_export_interval) OTEL_BSP_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE 4096 OTEL_BSP_SCHEDULE_DELAY 5000 OTEL_BSP_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE 512 OTEL_BSP_EXPORT_TIMEOUT 30000 OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES the profile's user ID, name, email, and team, URL-escaped (example below) NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS server.ca_cert_file, only with a private CA (below) 
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=user.id=alice,user.name=Alice%20Doe,user.profile.email=alice@example.com,user.team=platform

An attribute is left out when the profile field is empty.

cctrace owns these keys. If you had set any of them yourself, init overwrites it and reset removes it. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS is the exception, because it is often already set for a company proxy: cctrace records the value it writes in the cctrace object and changes or removes only that value. A value you set yourself stays, and if it differs from server.ca_cert_file, init and config set keep it and print both paths; put both CAs in one PEM file to use them together.

docs.title: Private CA
docs.text:
When the profile has server.ca_cert_file and the OTEL endpoint is https://, cctrace sends Claude Code over http/protobuf to the OTLP/HTTP port beside the gRPC one (4317 to 4318, 5317 to 5318) and sets NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS to the CA file. server.protocol stays as stored, and init and config set print one line saying so. Without a CA, or on plain http://, nothing changes.

The reason is a measurement with Claude Code 2.1.291 on macOS against a server certificate from a private CA:

Protocol CA given through Result grpc OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE (settings or process env) TLS handshake aborted: CA not trusted grpc NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS (settings or process env) same failure http/protobuf OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE (settings env) same failure http/protobuf NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS (process env) metrics and logs arrived http/protobuf NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS (settings env) metrics and logs arrived

Whether grpc trusts a CA installed in the OS keychain was not measured.

docs.title: Session hooks
docs.text:
When session log sync is enabled (options.sync_enabled), two hooks are added under hooks, each in the group with an empty matcher:

{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "/usr/local/bin/cctrace sync --daemon --log-to-file --claude-dir /Users/alice/.claude --auto-profile --interval 1s"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "SessionEnd": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "/usr/local/bin/cctrace sync --daemon --once --log-to-file --claude-dir /Users/alice/.claude --auto-profile",
            "async": true,
            "timeout": 30
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
  • The command starts with the absolute path of the binary that wrote it. A binary in a temporary directory is not used; cctrace falls back to the cctrace found on PATH. After moving the binary, run cctrace env apply.
  • --claude-dir is the profile's Claude home, and --auto-profile selects the matching profile. See Sync daemon for the flags.
  • SessionStart starts the daemon for the profile. SessionEnd runs one more pass, asynchronously with a 30-second timeout, and leaves the daemon running.
  • Existing hooks are kept. If a cctrace hook is already present, it is updated in place instead of added again.

Turning options.sync_enabled off later does not remove the hooks; the hook then runs and exits without syncing. cctrace reset removes them.

docs.title: Self-heal stamp
docs.text: cctrace also writes a top-level cctrace object holding a hash of what it generated. Each time the sync daemon starts, it recomputes the hash; if an upgraded binary would write different variables or hooks, it rewrites the settings file. reset removes the object.

docs.title: When changes take effect
docs.text: Claude Code reads the environment and hooks when a session starts. After init, env apply, or config set, start a new Claude Code session. A session that was already running sends no telemetry, and its session log is uploaded only from the point the daemon first sees it.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text: cctrace collects Codex CLI through OTEL metrics that Codex sends to the server, and through the session files that the sync daemon uploads.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
Run Codex once so that ~/.codex exists, then run cctrace init. When init finds that directory it asks:

  Codex CLI detected (~/.codex found).
  Enable Codex session sync? [Y/n]

Answering yes sets options.codex_sync_enabled in the profile and writes an [otel] section into ~/.codex/config.toml.

If you installed Codex after init, run cctrace init again and choose Patch Codex integration only. It keeps the existing endpoints and token, turns the option on, and writes the [otel] section without asking for your password.

init looks for the Codex home at CODEX_CONFIG_DIR when that variable is set, and at ~/.codex otherwise.

Codex is turned on automatically, unless you turned it off

Every sync run checks for the Codex home. If it exists, the profile has an OTEL endpoint and an upload token, and options.codex_sync_enabled is off, the sync turns the option on and writes the [otel] section. This covers profiles created before Codex support.

Answering no during init, or running cctrace config set options.codex_sync_enabled false, is recorded in the profile as options.codex_sync_declined, and the sync then leaves every Codex home alone. Running cctrace config set options.codex_sync_enabled true, accepting the prompt in init, or choosing Patch Codex integration only clears it.

docs.title: OTEL configuration
docs.text:
The section cctrace writes looks like this:

[otel]
metrics_exporter = { otlp-http = { endpoint = "http://cctrace.company.example:4318/v1/metrics", protocol = "binary", headers = { Authorization = "Bearer <upload token>", X-Cctrace-Codex-Account = "<account id>" } } }
  • The endpoint is derived from the profile's OTEL endpoint: port 4317 becomes 4318 (5317 becomes 5318 for the TLS overlay), and the path becomes /v1/metrics. Codex sends over OTLP/HTTP, not gRPC.
  • Only a metrics exporter is configured. cctrace sets up no OTEL log export for Codex.
  • X-Cctrace-Codex-Account carries the Codex billing account id from <Codex home>/auth.json, so the server can apply billing-account exclusions to Codex metrics. It is left out when the account is unknown and rewritten by the sync when the account changes. Codex reads the new section when it restarts.
  • With server.ca_cert_file set, the exporter gets tls = { ca-certificate = "<file>" }. Codex needs it to reach an https:// endpoint whose certificate comes from a private CA: without it Codex sends no metrics and reports no error. init, the Codex patch and the sync print a [!] warning when they write an https:// endpoint with no CA set. Whether Codex reaches an https:// endpoint with a publicly trusted certificate and no CA set was not measured.
  • cctrace manages the whole section and may add further headers to it. Any existing [otel] section, in inline or table form, is replaced. The rest of the file is kept. The file is replaced atomically and written with mode 0600.
  • On each sync run the section is compared with what the current profile would produce and rewritten if it differs, for example after you change the OTEL endpoint or server.ca_cert_file with cctrace config set. A tls table added by hand is removed when the profile has no CA.

docs.title: Session files
docs.text:
The sync daemon uploads Codex session files that match either of these under each Codex home:

sessions/rollout-*.jsonl
sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl

Codex homes scanned, in order, with duplicates removed:

  1. CODEX_CONFIG_DIR, or ~/.codex
  2. CODEX_HOME, when set (in addition to the default, not instead of it)
  3. Each directory in options.codex_dirs

The sync also rewrites the [otel] section of the extra homes (2 and 3) to the current format and that home's account header, but only while Codex sync is on and only when the home's [otel] endpoint already points at this cctrace server (same host and port). A home without an [otel] section is not touched, one that points at another server is named in the log and left alone, and a <Codex home>/config.toml that is a symbolic link is skipped with a message. The sync keeps the Bearer token already in an extra home and prints a line suggesting cctrace init when it differs from the profile's. cctrace init and the Codex patch replace it with the profile's token.

A directory in options.codex_dirs that does not exist is skipped with a message in the log. cctrace sync --dry-run lists the homes a real sync would scan and how many session files each holds.

Setting CCTRACE_CODEX_SYNC=true in the environment of the sync process also enables Codex collection, regardless of the profile option.

docs.title: Starting collection
docs.text:
Codex has no session hook. Its files are collected by whichever sync daemon is running for the profile:

  • If you also use Claude Code with the same profile, the daemon that Claude Code's SessionStart hook starts collects Codex too.
  • If you use only Codex, start the daemon yourself with cctrace sync --daemon, or run cctrace sync periodically.

As with every agent, the first pass skips content that is already on disk, so Synced 0 records right after enabling Codex is expected. Collection starts with content written after that.

docs.title: Removing the configuration
docs.text: cctrace reset and cctrace uninstall do not change ~/.codex/config.toml. Delete the [otel] section yourself to stop Codex from sending metrics.

docs.title: GJC and OMO
docs.text: cctrace collects GJC and OMO sessions by uploading their session files with the sync daemon. Neither agent is configured for OTEL, and neither gets a session hook.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
Run the agent once so that its home directory exists (~/.gjc or ~/.omo), then run cctrace init. For each directory it finds, init asks:

  gjc detected (~/.gjc found).
  Enable gjc session sync? [Y/n]

Answering yes sets options.gjc_sync_enabled or options.omo_sync_enabled in the profile. Nothing is written into the agent's own configuration.

To turn either on after init:

$ cctrace config set options.gjc_sync_enabled true
$ cctrace config set options.omo_sync_enabled true

Setting CCTRACE_GJC_SYNC=true or CCTRACE_OMO_SYNC=true in the environment of the sync process has the same effect, regardless of the profile option.

docs.title: Starting collection
docs.text:
Enabling the option does not start anything. The files are collected by whichever sync daemon runs for the profile:

  • If you also use Claude Code with the same profile, the daemon started by its SessionStart hook collects GJC and OMO too.
  • Otherwise start one yourself with cctrace sync --daemon or cctrace sync --watch, or run cctrace sync periodically.

The first pass skips content already on disk, so sessions from before you enabled the option are not uploaded.

docs.title: Files read
docs.text:
Homes scanned: ~/.gjc plus each directory in options.gjc_dirs for GJC, and ~/.omo plus each directory in options.omo_dirs for OMO. Under each home, these files are read:

GJC   agent/sessions/v2-*/*.jsonl        session files
      agent/sessions/v2-*/*/*.jsonl      subagent transcripts
OMO   sessions/--*--/*.jsonl
      agent/sessions/--*--/*.jsonl

A configured directory that does not exist is skipped with a message in the log. cctrace sync --dry-run lists the homes a real sync would scan and how many session files each holds.

Sync progress is kept in ~/.cctrace/gjc-sync-state.json and ~/.cctrace/omo-sync-state.json (or the named profile's directory).

docs.title: Install
docs.text: Build the cctrace client from source and put it on your PATH. Every developer machine that should report sessions needs one.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Go 1.26 or later (go.mod)
  • make
  • A running server. See Server install.

The client does not need Node.js or Docker. Those are only for the server and its dashboard.

docs.title: Build the client
docs.text:
make build-client builds one client for the current platform into dist/. Unlike make build, it does not need the dashboard build and runs on Linux as well as macOS.

make build-client

To build for another platform, use make build-linux (linux/amd64) or make build-windows (windows/amd64). Both also write into dist/.

Automatic updates are off by default

A client built from this repository without an update public key refuses automatic updates. To upgrade it, rebuild and replace the binary yourself. See Upgrading the client. A client built with your own update public key, from a signed server image or with make, can update itself; see Security operations.

Default endpoints for a team build

cctrace init asks for the server's sync and OTEL endpoints. To pre-fill those prompts in the binaries you hand out, copy deploy/local-defaults.env.example to a file named local-defaults.env in the same directory, set DEFAULT_SYNC_ENDPOINT and DEFAULT_OTEL_ENDPOINT, then rebuild. Without that file the prompts start empty and each user types both addresses. That file is read only by make. For the binaries the server image serves (below), pass --build-arg DEFAULT_SYNC_ENDPOINT=... and --build-arg DEFAULT_OTEL_ENDPOINT=... to docker build instead.

docs.title: Download from your own server
docs.text:
The server image built in Server install also cross-compiles the client and serves it from the server. If your machine can reach the server, you can download the client instead of building it:

Platform Path on the server macOS, Apple silicon /downloads/cctrace-darwin-arm64 macOS, Intel /downloads/cctrace-darwin-amd64 Linux, x86-64 /downloads/cctrace-linux-amd64 Linux, ARM64 /downloads/cctrace-linux-arm64 Windows, x86-64 /downloads/cctrace-windows-amd64.exe

The paths are served at the address you use as the sync endpoint in cctrace init, including its port. Replace <sync endpoint> below with that address, and <platform> with your platform's filename suffix from the table above (for example linux-amd64):

$ curl -fL -o cctrace "<sync endpoint>/downloads/cctrace-<platform>"
$ chmod +x cctrace

Use HTTPS or a network you trust for this download. If the server's certificate comes from a private CA (the Caddy tls internal default in Install the server), curl does not trust it yet; add --cacert cctrace-ca.crt.

These binaries are built with version dev unless the server image was built with --build-arg VERSION=.... cctrace --version then prints dev, and cctrace status marks the binary as a development build. They update themselves only when the server image was built signed, with your own keys and a release VERSION; see Security operations.

docs.title: Put it on PATH
docs.text:
Put the binary where it will stay before you run cctrace init. The Claude Code hooks that init writes call the binary by the absolute path it was run from, so a hook written while running it from dist/ or from your download directory keeps pointing there. If you move the binary later, run cctrace env apply from the new location to rewrite the hooks.

If you built it, the binary is dist/cctrace; if you downloaded it, it is cctrace in the directory you ran curl from:

$ sudo cp dist/cctrace /usr/local/bin/cctrace   # built with make build-client
$ sudo cp ./cctrace /usr/local/bin/cctrace      # downloaded from the server
$ cctrace --version
cctrace version dev

If you skip this, init offers to do it. When cctrace init finishes and cctrace is not on PATH, it asks:

  [!] 'cctrace' is not in $PATH. Install to /usr/local/bin? (y/n) [y]:
  • macOS and Linux: it copies the running binary to /usr/local/bin/cctrace. If the copy fails for lack of permission, it retries with sudo.
  • Windows: it copies the binary into AppData\Local\Programs\cctrace under your home directory and adds that directory to your user Path. Open a new terminal afterwards.

If you answer no, or the copy fails, init prints manual options instead: go install ./cmd/cctrace (then add ~/go/bin to PATH), or copying the binary into a directory that is already on PATH.

The copy happens after init has written the hooks, so they still name the binary init was run from. Run cctrace env apply once from the installed copy afterwards.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect the client to your server.

docs.title: Per-home transmission onboarding
docs.text:
The multi-home onboarding change is under implementation and validation; check support in the installed release before relying on it.

  1. Review discovered standard and additional Claude/Codex homes and select enrollment targets.
  2. Explicitly allow or exclude session uploads for every selected home.
  3. Review initial assignment: allowed homes to default, excluded homes to personal.
  4. Review separate usage-monitoring choices and which collection jobs will start.
  5. Complete server setup and final confirmation before collection starts for approved homes.

Discovery alone never starts collection for a new home. Upload exclusion does not hide or unregister the home or account. After onboarding, membership, upload exclusion, collection execution, and usage monitoring are independent. Allowing uploads in a stopped personal profile neither moves the home nor starts collection.

Both exclusion directions require confirmation showing affected homes, account, and profiles. Cancel preserves settings. Homes without usable credentials remain listed with their actual state.

docs.title: Local analysis
docs.text:
Local analysis shows the Claude Code and Codex CLI sessions stored on this machine in the dashboard, without needing a server. cctrace opens a small API on a loopback address that reads the session files, and a dashboard page in your browser connects to it with an address and a token.

The API itself sends nothing to a server, and it needs neither a server login nor a database. It does not replace the sync daemon.

docs.title: Two ways to run it
docs.text: cctrace local serve cctrace local enable Runs as A foreground command, until you press Ctrl-C Part of the profile's sync daemon Port Chosen by the operating system at each start, unless --address sets one Chosen when you run enable; the same on every daemon start Token New on every start, printed once New on every enable, printed once; only its hash is stored Pages allowed One or more --origin values The one --origin value Folders read The defaults below, or the ones you name The profile's Claude home and the Codex homes its daemon scans Needs a profile No Yes

docs.title: Run it once
docs.text:
cctrace local serve --origin http://127.0.0.1:8080

--origin is required. It is the exact origin of the dashboard page that will connect, written as the browser shows it: scheme, host, and the port when the page uses a non-default one, with no path and no trailing slash. For a dashboard behind a proxy, such as https://cctrace.company.example, give that address instead. Repeat --origin to allow more than one page. A wildcard, a path, a query string, or credentials in the origin are refused.

The first line of output is a JSON object. A second line says the API is active and that the token must stay private.

  • endpoint: the loopback address and port the API listens on
  • token: the bearer token for this run
  • profile_fingerprint: an identifier for the set of folders being read
  • origins: the allowed origins

The token is 32 random bytes, new on every start. Do not redirect the output to a file, put the token in a URL, or paste it into a report. Press Ctrl-C to stop the API; the token stops working with it.

Flag Default Effect --origin <origin> none, required Origin of a dashboard page allowed to call the API. Repeatable. --address <ip:port> 127.0.0.1:0 Address to listen on. It must be a literal loopback IP address; a name such as localhost is refused. Port 0 lets the operating system choose. --claude-dir <dir> see below Claude config directory to read. Repeatable. --codex-dir <dir> see below Codex home to read. Repeatable.

docs.title: Folders it reads
docs.text:
Without --claude-dir or --codex-dir, serve reads these folders:

  • Claude Code: the folder CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR names, or ~/.claude, and the Claude home of each profile that sets one.
  • Codex CLI: CODEX_CONFIG_DIR, or ~/.codex; CODEX_HOME when it is set; and the Codex home of each profile that sets one. The profile option options.codex_dirs is not consulted.

A folder that does not exist is skipped. Passing either flag switches off all of the above: serve then reads only the folders you name and adds no profile's folders. With --claude-dir alone no Codex session is read, and the reverse.

Inside a Claude folder the API reads JSONL session files under projects; inside a Codex folder, the rollout files under sessions (the layout in Codex CLI). A file that resolves to a place outside its folder is ignored, and a symbolic link in place of the projects or sessions directory is not followed.

docs.title: Run it with the daemon
docs.text:
cctrace local enable --origin https://cctrace.company.example

Add --profile <name> to act on a named profile. enable prints a JSON object with endpoint and token once. It stores the origin, a free port on 127.0.0.1, and the SHA-256 hash of the token (not the token) in the profile directory: ~/.cctrace/local-api-policy.json for the default profile, ~/.cctrace/profiles/<name>/local-api-policy.json for a named one. It also turns on the profile option options.local_analysis_enabled.

The API starts together with the profile's sync daemon, so restart a daemon that was already running (cctrace sync --stop, then cctrace sync --daemon). It reads that profile's Claude home and the Codex homes the daemon scans, listed in Codex CLI. If the stored port is taken when the daemon starts, the API does not start and status reports the error. enable does not change the profile's sync settings: the daemon keeps uploading as the profile's options say.

cctrace local status
cctrace local disable

status prints one JSON object: enabled, running, origin, address, generation, started_at, ended_at, and error. disable clears the stored token hash and turns the option off, and a running daemon stops the API when it notices.

Running enable again issues a new token and a new port. The previous token stops working and the running daemon stops its API, so restart the daemon to start it with the new values.

docs.title: Connect from the dashboard
docs.text:
Two pages use the connection:

  • /local-sessions works without signing in to the dashboard.
  • The 내 기기와 서버 view on the Sessions page needs a signed-in dashboard session, because it lists server sessions next to the local ones.

Open the page at the origin you gave to --origin. Enter the endpoint value in 로컬 서비스 주소 and the token in 접속 토큰, then press 연결. The form accepts only http:// followed by localhost, 127.0.0.1, or [::1] and a port, and it rewrites localhost to 127.0.0.1 before it connects. The API accepts only the exact address it listens on. Type the endpoint value as printed: an address with 127.0.0.1 in endpoint is refused if you write [::1] instead.

이 탭에 연결 저장 keeps the address and token in the sessionStorage of that browser tab, so a reload reconnects without pasting them again. Closing the tab forgets them. Without the box checked, the token stays in the page's memory and a reload asks for it again. 연결 끊기 clears the saved pair.

The session list has a search box and an agent filter (전체, Claude, Codex). Token counts, event counts and cost in the list show 미집계 (not tallied) instead of zero, because the list reads only the first and last 32 KiB of each file. Selecting a session opens three tabs: 대화, 개별 원문, and 분석. The analysis tab reads the whole file and computes what the records support; a value they cannot support stays empty.

In the 내 기기와 서버 view, a local session and a server session with the same session ID are listed apart. The page offers 같은 세션으로 묶기 to group them by hand, because the same ID alone does not show that both belong to the same person.

docs.title: What the API allows
docs.text:
• It listens on a loopback address only. serve refuses any other --address, and enable always uses 127.0.0.1.
  • Every request except a browser's CORS preflight needs the token. The Host header must equal the listen address, which refuses a request that reaches the API under another name, such as a DNS-rebinding page.
  • A request that carries an Origin header outside the allowed list is refused.
  • It reads session files and does not modify them. The one write is the choice of profile for the next Claude Code or Codex run, which a page can save through serve, stored in ~/.cctrace/next-profile.json; the daemon's API has no profile choice.
  • It does not check whether a local session also exists on the server, or who owns it.
  • Responses are marked no-store.

An HTTPS dashboard page may need the browser's local network permission before it can reach a loopback address. Allowing an origin in the CLI does not grant that permission, and does not show that every browser supports the connection.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Use one profile per Claude config directory when you run Claude Code with more than one account on the same machine.

docs.title: How profiles map to accounts
docs.text:
Claude Code keeps each login in its own config directory: ~/.claude by default, or another directory selected with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR. cctrace follows the same split.

Profile Stored in Claude home Default ~/.cctrace/profile.json ~/.claude Named, for example work ~/.cctrace/profiles/work/profile.json The directory the profile names, for example ~/.claude-work

Each profile carries its own server endpoints, cctrace user identity, upload token, and options, and writes its OTEL variables and hooks into the settings file of its own Claude home. The sync daemon, its lock, its log, and its sync state are also per profile. See Sync daemon.

Which cctrace user a profile reports as depends on how it was created:

  • cctrace init --profile <name> authenticates on its own, so the profile can belong to a different cctrace user than the default one.
  • cctrace profile add and the directories init detects copy the default profile's user, server, and options. They report as the same cctrace user.

Profile names must start with a letter or digit and may contain letters, digits, - and _ (up to 63 characters). default is reserved.

docs.title: Automatic detection during init
docs.text:
At the end of cctrace init for the default profile, init looks for directories in your home directory whose name starts with .claude- and that contain a projects directory or a settings file (settings.json). .claude-mem is ignored, as is any directory another profile already uses.

  Detected 2 additional Claude home(s):
    1. /Users/alice/.claude-work
    2. /Users/alice/.claude-personal

  Set up sync for which? (all/none/1,2,...) [all]:

For each directory you pick, init creates a named profile whose name is the directory name without the leading dot (claude-work), copies the default profile into it, and writes that directory's settings file.

docs.title: Add a profile
docs.text:
$ cctrace profile add claude-4 --home ~/.claude-4

profile add copies the default profile, points it at the directory given by --home, and writes the OTEL variables and hooks into that directory's settings file. --home is required. The default profile must exist first.

It refuses a name that already exists and a Claude home that another named profile already uses. If the directory does not exist yet, it warns and creates the profile anyway.

To set up a profile with its own login instead, run init with a name:

$ cctrace init --profile work

This runs the full setup and adds one prompt, Claude config directory (Enter for default ~/.claude). init warns if another profile already uses the directory you enter.

docs.title: List profiles
docs.text:
cctrace profile list

Prints the default profile (once it is set up) and each named profile with its Claude home. cctrace status shows both too.

docs.title: Remove a profile
docs.text:
cctrace profile remove work

Deletes the directory under ~/.cctrace/profiles/ for that profile after asking for confirmation (--force skips it). It does not touch the profile's Claude settings file, so the OTEL variables and hooks stay there. To remove those as well, use cctrace reset --profile work instead. See Reset and uninstall.

If the profile held a source that other profiles share, no profile collects that source afterwards until one claims it; see Source folders that profiles share.

docs.title: Select a profile on the command line
docs.text:
Commands that act on one profile take --profile <name>: status, config (including config policy), env apply, sync, kill, reset, local enable, local status, and local disable. sync, kill, and config policy also read the CCTRACE_PROFILE environment variable when the flag is not given.

The hooks written into a Claude home pass --claude-dir with that home and --auto-profile. --auto-profile picks the named profile whose Claude home matches the --claude-dir value (or, without that flag, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR). When no named profile matches, the default profile is used.

docs.title: Source folders that profiles share
docs.text:
Two profiles can end up reading the same source folder. The usual case is the default Codex home: every profile with Codex collection turned on scans it when it exists. The daemon treats a folder as shared when the profiles upload to the same destination, meaning the same sync endpoint, cctrace user, and email, and the folders their collectors read are the same, or one lies inside the other. Uploading such a folder from both profiles would count every session in it twice, so the daemon lets one profile collect it.

  • One profile collects it. That profile is the holder. The first profile the daemon gives a source to keeps it, whatever the other profiles do afterwards. On a first start the default profile goes first, then the named profiles in name order. A profile that is stopped or turned off is not given new sources, but keeps the ones it holds.
  • The other profile loses only that source. Everything else it collects keeps uploading: its Claude sessions and every folder it does not share. The profile is not paused as a whole, unless every one of its sources is shared. Then it collects nothing, and cctrace status says so.
  • The holder's filters apply. A shared source is sent as the holder's filters allow (repository allowlist, prompt and tool redaction, excluded accounts). The held-back profile sends nothing from it, so its own filters never widen what is sent.
  • The held-back period is not caught up on. A profile that starts with no saved progress at all skips the sessions already on disk and collects new ones. A profile that already has saved progress, such as one that read the source before, goes on from it, so it can send files of the held-back period too, some of which another profile has already sent; the server drops the duplicates. When a source changes hands, the new holder continues from the old holder's progress where the daemon can read it; otherwise it skips the sessions already on disk and collects new ones.
  • The holder changes only when you change it, with one exception. A holder that is stopped or turned off still holds its sources, and a profile you remove leaves its sources unread by every profile, so that a removal never hands them to a profile with other filters. If the holder takes a source out of its own settings, for example by turning that agent's collection off, it lets the source go, and the next profile whose filters are the same or stricter takes it over by itself. If none qualifies, nobody collects the source until you run cctrace profile claim. If a change on disk, such as replacing a folder with a link to another folder, makes two sources that different profiles hold into one, the hold made first stays and the other profile is held back from it, once it has stopped reading that source.

When the shared folders are the same folder, nothing is lost: the holder reads every file in it. When one lies inside the other, the daemon still keeps just one profile on it, but some files may be collected by no profile at all, because a collector reads only certain depths of a folder. cctrace status marks such a row with a warning.

docs.title: See what is held back
docs.text:
cctrace status prints a 수집 경로 line for a profile only when it is held back from a source. The output is in Korean:

    수집 경로:     [!] 이 프로필에서 수집하지 않는 경로 2개 -- 같은 서버·사용자로 수집하는 다른 프로필이 맡고 있습니다
                   codex  기본 폴더        3fa91c2d  맡은 프로필: default (수집 중)
                   codex  [명시 Codex 홈]  9b01d7e4  맡은 프로필: personal (중지됨)
                   나머지 경로는 정상 수집합니다. 맡길 프로필을 바꾸려면: cctrace profile claim <프로필> --source <id>

Each row is the kind of source, where its folder came from, its id, and the holder with its state. The folder is never printed as a path.

Column Values Folder 홈 폴더 (Claude home), 기본 폴더 (default Codex home), CODEX_HOME, 설정 폴더 (a folder in the profile's settings), [명시 Codex 홈] (the profile's explicit Codex home) Holder state 수집 중 (collecting), 중지됨 (stopped), 꺼짐 (turned off), 막힘 (blocked), 이전 중 (handing the source over) Holder missing (삭제됨) (removed profile), (주인 없음) (nobody holds it), (알 수 없음) (unknown)

A row ends with -- 일부 파일은 어느 프로필에도 수집되지 않을 수 있음 (some files may be collected by no profile) when the folders are nested. When every source of the profile is shared, the first line reads [!] 이 프로필의 모든 경로가 다른 프로필과 겹쳐 수집이 멈춰 있습니다 (duplicate_route). When the profile began a folder only after it was let in, a last line reads 겹침으로 막혀 있던 기간의 세션은 수집되지 않았습니다 (수집을 시작한 시점부터 수집) (the sessions of the held-back period were not collected; collection starts from when it began). cctrace sync status and the daemon log show the same facts for all profiles at once; see Sync daemon.

docs.title: Give a shared source to another profile
docs.text:
$ cctrace profile claim work --source 3fa91c2d
$ cctrace profile claim work --all --force

profile claim <profile> moves sources the profile is held back from to the profile. The holder lets go first, then <profile> starts reading from the holder's progress. The local daemon must be running (cctrace sync --daemon); the command says so and stops when it is not.

Flag Meaning --source <id\|folder> A source to claim: the id from cctrace status, or its folder in any spelling of the same folder. Repeatable. --all Every source the profile is held back from --force Skip the confirmation

With neither --source nor --all, the command lists what the profile is held back from and stops. For each source it prints a plan and asks Proceed? [y/N]. Without a terminal, it refuses unless you pass --force.

Claim codex source 3fa91c2d (default folder) for profile "work"
  current holder : default (active)
  cursor         : continue from "default"
  filters        : repository allowlist: default 2 entries, "work" none (collects every repository)
                   prompt redaction: default off, "work" off
                   tool redaction: default off, "work" off
                   excluded accounts: default 0, "work" 0
                   note: "work" would send more than "default" does
  effect         : "default" stops reading this source; "work" starts after "default" has released it
Proceed? [y/N]

Read the filters lines before you confirm. They compare how many entries each profile's filters hold and whether each is on, never their values, because a repository prefix is a path. The note line appears when the profile taking the source would send more than the holder does. Where the holder's progress cannot be read, cursor reads holder state unavailable; existing sessions will be skipped, new ones collected. For a source nobody holds because its holder took it out of its settings, the progress is that of the profile that read it last, and cursor reads continue from that profile.

After the daemon accepts a claim, the command prints Claim 3fa91c2d accepted: "default" lets go of it first, then "work" starts reading it. The move finishes in the background. If the daemon refuses, for example because a hand-over of that source is still in progress, nothing changes and the message says what to do. A source whose holder is removed, or that nobody holds, is claimed at once. While the routes file cannot be used (the daemon logs [routes] invalid), the first claim has the daemon rebuild it, and --all or several --source flags still claim every source you name: before each further one, the command waits, up to ten seconds, for the daemon to publish the rebuilt file.

docs.title: Server policy deferral
docs.text:
A server operator can publish a signed policy that moves clients to new server addresses. Only a client built with an update public key or a policy public key applies one (see Sync daemon). Nothing below applies to a client built from this repository without an update or policy public key.

A policy rewrites files that two profiles can share: the Claude settings file in a profile's Claude home and the Codex configuration file in the default Codex home, in the directory CODEX_HOME names when it is set, and in each directory of options.codex_dirs. When another profile uses one of the same files, the client defers the policy instead of applying it, unless the file is a Codex configuration file and either every profile that uses it moves to the same server or it is the one in the default Codex home (see below). The run ends with an error that ends in policy deferred, the profile keeps its current addresses and keeps collecting, and every later check ends the same way until the file is no longer shared. cctrace config policy status prints the reason.

The client checks every other profile, the default profile first and then the named profiles by name, and does not stop at the first conflict. The reason lists each conflict as a profile name and a kind of file, ordered by name, and Claude before Codex for the same profile:

shared settings with profiles "home" (claude), "work" (codex); policy deferred
Entry Cause "<name>" (claude) The other profile has the same Claude home. <name> is empty when the other profile is the default profile. "<name>" (codex) Both profiles scan a Codex directory in common other than the default Codex home, one named by CODEX_HOME or listed in options.codex_dirs, and Codex sync has not been turned off for either. Listed only when that profile does not move with this one. Earlier client versions list a profile that shares only the default Codex home too, which every profile scans when that folder exists.

The reason holds at most 500 characters. When too many profiles conflict to name them all, the last entries are counted instead: ... and 31 more; policy deferred. The number counts entries, not profiles, so a profile that conflicts on both counts twice. Earlier client versions stop at the first conflict and report it alone, as shared Claude settings with profile "<name>"; policy deferred or shared Codex settings with profile "<name>"; policy deferred.

A profile that shares a Codex configuration file moves with this one, and is not listed, when it already uses the policy's new addresses, or when the policy names it with the addresses it uses now and its sync daemon is running in a state the policy can restart: started without --local or --endpoint, and reading its own Claude home. A different spelling of the same server, another port, or another protocol is not an address the policy names. A shared Claude home always defers the policy, even when the other profile moves too. Earlier client versions defer on every shared Codex configuration file.

When profiles move together, the client writes the shared Codex configuration file after the policy is committed rather than with it, and keeps the write in its policy state until it is done: the file's path, digests of the old and new [otel] sections, the old OTEL address, and the old certificate path. The record holds no token. Each later run carries the write out before it asks the server for a policy. If a file outside the default Codex home holds an [otel] section that none of the moving profiles writes, the run is deferred with shared Codex settings edited; policy deferred until the file holds one of theirs again. If the write fails, the run ends with shared settings write pending and the next run tries again. A session of the other profile can put its old section back before that profile applies the policy; once it applies, the file uses the new server.

The Codex configuration file in the default Codex home is the exception. Every profile with Codex sync turned on writes its own [otel] section there whenever its sync runs, and the profile that wrote last wins, whatever a policy does, so no policy can hold that file still for the others. A profile that shares only that file with others does not defer the policy, whether the others move or not. The profile moves, and the file is handled by what it holds:

The file holds The client This profile's old section Writes the new section after the policy is committed, as above. This profile's new section, or a section of a profile that moves with it Changes nothing. A section of a profile that does not move, a section edited by hand, or anything else Leaves the file as it is and still moves the profile.

The token in the section never changes: a policy moves the server and keeps the credentials. When the file is left as it is, the policy still counts as applied and the run ends with the check result ok. The reason, in cctrace config policy status and in the report to the server, reads default Codex config kept: <path>. Until this profile's sync next starts and writes its own section, which carries the new address, that file keeps sending Codex metrics wherever its current section points, under that section's token. When several profiles use the default Codex home, Codex metrics go to the server of whichever of them wrote last, as before a policy; a policy does not change that. Earlier client versions defer on this file like any other.

A profile's explicit Codex home (codex_home) is written by that profile alone, so it is not a shared file and never defers a policy. With Codex sync turned on for the profile, the client moves the home's [otel] section in the same transaction as the rest of the policy, and only when the section is what cctrace generates for the profile: on the address the profile uses now, or on an address the policy moves from on the same host, naming the profile's certificate, the certificate the user supplied before any policy, or none. The one difference is the token: the section keeps the token it carries, which may be one that belongs to no profile on this machine. The rest of the file is kept as it is. A home that is also the default Codex home, the directory CODEX_HOME names, or a directory in options.codex_dirs follows the rule of that directory above.

The explicit home's file holds The client This profile's section as described above Writes the new section with the policy. A section already on the policy's new address, a section with the token of another profile whose own policy run reaches this home (it scans the folder, or has it as its explicit home with Codex sync on), or no file Changes nothing and says nothing. The other profile moves its own section. No [otel] section, a section that sends elsewhere or was edited by hand, a section in an older form or a multi-line root otel key, a file that cannot be read, a Codex configuration file that is a symlink, a section with the token of a profile whose policy run does not reach this home, or a home whose lock the client cannot take Leaves the file as it is and still moves the profile.

When the file is left as it is, the policy counts as applied and the run ends with the check result ok. The reason, in cctrace config policy status and in the report to the server, reads explicit Codex home kept, joined with ; to the default Codex home's note when both apply. A path of an explicit Codex home in any reason a policy run records or reports is replaced by [explicit Codex home]. A lock that another process holds is waited for like any other, and ends the run when the wait runs out. If writing the file fails, the whole transaction is rolled back, the policy is not applied, and the next check tries again.

To separate the Claude settings, give one of the two profiles its own Claude home:

$ cctrace profile edit work --home ~/.claude-work
$ cctrace env apply --profile work

profile edit changes only the profile's folders, and env apply writes the OTEL variables and hooks into the new home. Alternatively, remove the profile and add it again with --home. Removing a profile also deletes a login it had of its own. The new profile copies the default profile's user, server, and options, and its sync state starts empty, so it skips content already on disk.

To separate the Codex settings of a directory other than the default Codex home, turn Codex sync off for all but one of the profiles. Turning it off stops that profile's Codex collection:

$ cctrace config set options.codex_sync_enabled false --profile work

Two more reasons also keep a policy deferred until the file's owner changes it: the certificate file the client wrote for an earlier policy no longer matches what it wrote, or server.ca_cert_file no longer points to it (managed CA was edited; policy deferred or managed CA was changed; policy deferred), and a Codex configuration file that no other profile uses has an [otel] section that differs from what cctrace generates for the profile (unmanaged Codex OTEL settings differ from the profile; policy deferred). With Codex sync turned off for the profile, the second no longer applies.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: Point the client at your server with cctrace init, restart your agent, and confirm collection with cctrace status.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The server is running and you know two addresses: the sync endpoint (HTTP, port 8080 by default) and the OTEL endpoint (gRPC, port 4317 by default). See Ports.
  • An administrator has created your account. See Users.
  • You have signed in to the dashboard once and replaced the temporary password. The server refuses CLI authentication while a temporary password is pending, and init stops with please change your password on the dashboard before authenticating.
  • Your account has a team. init takes your name, email, and team from the server and fails validation if any of them is empty.

docs.title: Run init
docs.text:
cctrace init

init asks for the following, in this order:

Prompt What to enter Sync endpoint The server's HTTP address, for example https://cctrace.company.example. A bare host:port gets http:// prepended. OTEL endpoint The server's OTLP gRPC address, for example http://cctrace.company.example:4317. CA certificate file (PEM) Asked only when either endpoint is https://. The root certificate of a private CA, such as the one exported in Install the server. Give it even if the OS keychain already trusts that CA: Claude Code takes it from NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS (over http/protobuf; see Claude Code) and Codex from its own configuration, both written by cctrace from this file, and whether the keychain alone is enough for them was not tested. Leave empty for a publicly trusted certificate (cctrace keeps the system roots; not tested with Codex). Type none to remove a stored CA; with both endpoints on http:// a stored CA is removed without asking. Stored as server.ca_cert_file. User ID Your cctrace user ID. If you type an email address, the part after @ is dropped. Temporary password Your current dashboard password (the one you set after the first sign-in). Input is hidden. Three attempts. Enable session log sync? (y/n) y (default) installs the Claude Code hooks that start the sync daemon. n leaves telemetry on and session logs off. Create a read token for analysis commands Only needed for the read commands, which are under active development. n is fine.

An empty endpoint is not accepted. If an endpoint is plain http:// to anything but this machine (localhost or a loopback address), init warns that transcripts or telemetry will cross the network unencrypted. Private and link-local addresses are warned about too. It does not refuse.

After authentication, init checks for other agents and asks about each one it finds:

  • ~/.codex exists: enable Codex session sync. See Codex CLI.
  • ~/.gjc or ~/.omo exists: enable GJC or OMO session sync. See GJC and OMO.

Finally, if it finds other Claude homes such as ~/.claude-work, it offers to create a profile for each. See Profiles.

docs.title: What init writes
docs.text:
File Change ~/.cctrace/profile.json Your profile: endpoints, user identity, upload token, options. Written with mode 0600. ~/.claude/settings.json OTEL environment variables under env, the SessionStart and SessionEnd hooks (when sync is enabled), and a cctrace stamp object. Other keys are left as they were. See Claude Code. ~/.codex/config.toml Only if you enabled Codex: an [otel] section.

A named profile (cctrace init --profile work) is written to ~/.cctrace/profiles/work/profile.json instead, and asks one more question: which Claude config directory it belongs to.

docs.title: Restart the agent
docs.text:
Claude Code reads the environment and hooks when a session starts, so the session you ran init from is not collected. Quit it and start a new one.

From the next session on:

  • Claude Code sends OTEL metrics and logs to the OTEL endpoint.
  • The SessionStart hook starts the sync daemon, which uploads session logs.

Content already on disk at the first sync, including earlier sessions, is not uploaded. To start the daemon now instead of waiting for a new session, run cctrace sync --daemon.

docs.title: Check the connection
docs.text:
cctrace status

status prints these sections:

Section Shows USER Name, email, user ID, team SERVER OTEL endpoint and whether it answers; sync endpoint; 서버 도달 (whether this status process reached the server) and 수집 상태 (whether the sync daemon's uploads are getting through); the start of the upload token PATHS Binary location, Claude home, Claude settings file path and whether it exists, profile directory OPTIONS Whether session log sync is on, and any redaction that is on NAMED PROFILES Each named profile, when you run status without --profile QUOTA Claude plan usage windows, fetched from Anthropic's usage API with the local Claude Code login. Unavailable on a machine that is not signed in to Claude Code; this does not affect collection.

status exits with code 1 when there is no profile and code 2 when the OTEL endpoint is unreachable. Use cctrace status --profile work for a named profile.

docs.title: Run init again
docs.text:
If a profile already exists, init offers a menu instead of starting over:

  Profile already exists: ...
    1) Patch Codex integration only (keep existing settings)
    2) Re-apply hooks and OTEL env for this binary (keep existing settings)
    3) Full re-setup (re-enter endpoint, password)
    4) Cancel

The Codex entry is listed only when ~/.codex exists; without it the other entries move up by one. Enter selects the first entry. Full re-setup backs up the profile first and restores it if setup fails.

docs.title: Re-apply hooks and environment
docs.text:
cctrace env apply

env apply rewrites the OTEL variables and hooks in the Claude settings file (~/.claude/settings.json, or the profile's Claude home) from the saved profile, using the path of the binary you run it with. Use it after you move or replace the binary.

Flag Effect --profile <name> Apply only this named profile --all Apply the default profile and every named profile

docs.title: View and change settings
docs.text:
cctrace config list
cctrace config get server.sync_endpoint
cctrace config set options.codex_sync_enabled true

cctrace config with no subcommand is the same as config list. Tokens are masked in the listing. Add --profile <name> to act on a named profile.

config set saves the profile and then rewrites the Claude settings file, so a change to endpoints, identity, or options reaches Claude Code the next time a session starts. Boolean values take true or false.

server.ca_cert_file is an exception in two ways. A running sync daemon keeps the CA it started with, so after setting or clearing it, restart the daemon: cctrace sync --stop, then start it again as usual (the next Claude Code session starts it, or cctrace sync --daemon). Codex's [otel] section is rewritten with the new CA when sync next starts, not by config set. The command prints both reminders.

user.id, user.name, user.email, user.team
server.endpoint                     OTEL endpoint
server.sync_endpoint                sync (HTTP) endpoint
server.protocol                     OTLP protocol for Claude Code (default grpc)
server.auth_token                   upload token issued by init
server.ca_cert_file                 private CA (PEM) the server's certificate comes from; "" clears it
options.sync_enabled                session log sync on or off
options.redact_user_prompts         replace conversation text (prompts and replies) before upload
options.redact_tool_details         drop tool arguments and results before upload
options.codex_sync_enabled          collect Codex CLI sessions
options.gjc_sync_enabled            collect GJC sessions
options.omo_sync_enabled            collect OMO sessions
options.metrics_export_interval     OTEL metric export interval in ms (default 60000)
options.logs_export_interval        OTEL log export interval in ms (default 5000)
options.collect_repository_prefixes repository id prefixes (host/org/repo) to collect, comma-separated; empty collects all
options.codex_dirs                  extra Codex homes to scan, comma-separated
options.gjc_dirs                    extra GJC homes to scan, comma-separated
options.omo_dirs                    extra OMO homes to scan, comma-separated

The *_dirs keys accept absolute paths or paths starting with ~, and each directory must already exist. An empty value clears the list.

config list also shows keys for areas that are under active development and are not documented here.

docs.title: Sync daemon
docs.text: The sync daemon uploads session logs from disk to the server's sync endpoint. OTEL telemetry does not go through it; the agents send that themselves.

docs.title: How it starts
docs.text:
With session log sync enabled, cctrace init installs two Claude Code hooks (see Claude Code):

Hook Runs Effect SessionStart cctrace sync --daemon ... --auto-profile --interval 1s Starts a background watch process for the profile, polling every second. If one is already running, the new one exits. SessionEnd cctrace sync --daemon --once ... --auto-profile Runs one extra pass in the background. The hook is asynchronous and does not stop the running daemon, which keeps serving other open sessions.

One daemon per profile collects every agent enabled in that profile: Claude Code, and Codex CLI, GJC, or OMO when their options are on. Codex, GJC, and OMO install no hook of their own. If you use only those agents, start the daemon yourself:

cctrace sync --daemon

The daemon prints its pid, its log path, and Stop: cctrace sync --stop.

docs.title: Run a sync by hand
docs.text:
cctrace sync                 # one pass, then exit
cctrace sync --watch         # stay in the foreground, one pass every 30s
cctrace sync --dry-run       # list new records per file without sending

cctrace sync with no profile, directory, or mode flags runs one pass for the default profile and then for each named profile.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Default Effect --watch off Keep running in the foreground and poll for new records --interval <duration> 30s Poll interval for watch mode, as a Go duration (30s, 2m). The installed hook uses 1s. --daemon off Start a background watch process and return --once off With --daemon: run one pass in the background and exit. Used by the SessionEnd hook. --stop off Ask the running daemon to finish its pass and exit. Waits up to 35 seconds. --dry-run off Show what would be sent, including which Codex, GJC, and OMO homes would be scanned. Sends nothing. --claude-dir <dir> profile's Claude home, else ~/.claude Claude config directory to read session logs from --profile <name> CCTRACE_PROFILE, else default profile Named profile to use --auto-profile off Pick the named profile whose Claude home matches --claude-dir, or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that flag is absent --profile-email <email> CCTRACE_PROFILE_EMAIL, else the profile's email Email attached to uploaded records --endpoint <url> profile's sync endpoint Send to this HTTP endpoint instead, for example http://localhost:8080 --local off Development use: send to a server on localhost. Reads CCTRACE_LOCAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and CCTRACE_LOCAL_OTEL_ENDPOINT, or HTTP_PORT and GRPC_PORT, from the environment or the nearest .env file in or above the current directory; otherwise uses ports 8080 and 4317.

The upload endpoint is chosen in this order: --endpoint, then the profile's sync endpoint, then its OTEL endpoint.

The hooks also pass a hidden --log-to-file flag, which sends the process's own output to the profile's log. You do not need it when running sync by hand.

docs.title: What gets uploaded
docs.text:
• Claude Code session logs under the Claude home's projects directory.
  • Codex CLI, GJC, and OMO session files, when enabled for the profile. See Codex CLI and GJC and OMO.

The first pass for each agent skips what is already on disk: every existing file is marked as read up to its current end, and only content written after that is uploaded. History from before the install is therefore not uploaded. The exception is the Claude Code session whose SessionStart hook started the daemon: it is read from the beginning. cctrace status reports how many files were skipped this way.

On every start, the daemon also compares the Claude settings file with what the current binary would write, and rewrites it if they differ.

When uploads fail, the daemon backs off before retrying (about 5 minutes at most, longer if the server asks for it). If sending has failed for 30 minutes because the server cannot be reached, and the SessionStart hook is installed, the daemon releases its lock and exits so that the next session starts a fresh one. Read offsets are kept, so nothing is lost.

docs.title: Sources shared between profiles
docs.text:
When two profiles that upload to the same destination share a source folder, the daemon lets one profile, the holder, collect the overlapping source and holds the other back from it. The rest of each profile keeps collecting. Which profile holds a source, how to move it, and what nested folders mean are in Profiles. A source is held back from the moment the daemon decides. A profile that starts with no saved progress at all skips the sessions of that period, as with the first-pass skip above. A profile that already has saved progress goes on from it, so it can send files of that period too; the server drops what it already has.

A one-shot cctrace sync, the SessionEnd pass, and re-enrichment follow the same decision. They read a source only when the running daemon would let that profile read it, and report one they leave out on stderr, or in the log for a background pass:

profile=work [routes] kind=codex source=3fa91c2d was not read: another profile holds it

A folder is judged by which folder it is, not by how it is spelled or where it came from. A folder given by a flag or an environment variable is left out too when it overlaps a source that the daemon's decision gives to another profile that uploads to the same destination. The line reads source=- when no source id is known, for example while the routes file cannot be used. These runs also leave out a source that was handed to the profile a moment ago (it was just handed to this profile, and the daemon reads it first): the daemon's job reads it first, from the previous holder's progress.

docs.title: cctrace sync status
docs.text:
cctrace sync status prints what the running daemon last published as a table; --json prints the raw snapshot instead. A section appears only when it has rows.

daemon   pid 4121   version 1.2.3   started 2026-10-15T09:12:03Z   observed 3s ago   complete yes

PROFILE   STATE    SENT  LAST PASS             NEXT RETRY  CODE
default   healthy  1204  2026-10-15T09:31:10Z  -           -
work      healthy   311  2026-10-15T09:31:08Z  -           -
personal  blocked     0  -                     -           duplicate_route

SHARED SOURCES (collected by another profile, not by the one on the left)
PROFILE   KIND    SOURCE    LABEL    REASON  HELD BY  HOLDER STATE
work      codex   3fa91c2d  default  same    default  active
personal  claude  77aa10c2  home     same    default  active
Column Meaning CODE duplicate_route when every source of the profile is shared, so the profile collects nothing SOURCE The source's id, as cctrace profile claim --source takes it LABEL Where the folder came from: home, default, env, configured, or explicit REASON same for one folder, nested for folders inside each other, where some files may be collected by no profile HELD BY, HOLDER STATE The holder, and active, stopped, disabled, blocked, transferring, removed, unowned, or unknown

A third section, DOWNGRADE, lists sources that an older build of the daemon could not represent, each with the command that clears it: cctrace profile claim <profile> --source <id>. It matters only if you go back to such a build.

docs.title: Daemon log
docs.text:
The daemon writes one [routes] line when a decision changes, not on every pass. A line carries names, counts, and ids, never a folder, an address, or a token. A state line, such as excluded, is written again only if the state ends and comes back.

Line Meaning [routes] reserved profile=default kind=codex source=3fa91c2d label=default destination=1a2b3c4d The profile now holds the source. destination is the first eight characters of a hash. [routes] excluded profile=work kind=codex source=3fa91c2d label=default reason=same holder=default holder_state=active The profile is held back from the source [routes] fully-shared profile=work sources=1 holders=default Every source of the profile is held back [routes] releasing source=3fa91c2d holder=default to=work cause=claim The holder is letting go of the source, to the named profile (to=none if nobody takes it), because of claim, source_removed, or collision [routes] releasing source=3fa91c2d holder=work to=none cause=collision Two sources that were held separately turned out to be one, for example after a folder was replaced by a link to another folder. The hold made later is let go of, and no profile reads the source until its holder has stopped reading it. [routes] released source=3fa91c2d holder=default cause=source_removed successor=none The holder let go and no profile took the source [routes] removed source=3fa91c2d holder=work cause=collision The holder of the later hold has stopped reading, and the hold was removed. The earlier hold's holder reads the source from now on. [routes] handoff source=3fa91c2d from=default to=work The source changed hands [routes] orphan source=3fa91c2d former_holder=default The holder was removed; nobody reads the source until a claim [routes] invalid reason=unreadable The routes file could not be used. Overlapping sources stay unread until cctrace profile claim rebuilds it. [routes] write-failed rev=8 reason=io The routes file could not be written, so the new decision is not applied and the write is tried again. The line is written once while the failure lasts. reason is io, or the word of the check that refused the file.

docs.title: Server policy
docs.text:
A server operator can publish one signed policy that moves a client to new server addresses and a new certificate authority. The client verifies it with the update public key or the policy public key linked into the binary, so only a client built with one of them applies a policy. A client built from this repository without an update or policy public key has neither (see Upgrading the client): it never starts a policy check by itself, and cctrace config policy apply run by hand fails with policy public key is not configured; rebuild with main.policyPublicKeyBase64 or main.updatePublicKeyBase64. A client built with your own public key, passed as the UPDATE_PUBLIC_KEY or POLICY_PUBLIC_KEY Make variable or Docker build argument, applies a policy signed with the matching private key.

A client with the key starts a background policy check, cctrace config policy apply, from cctrace sync at three points:

  • when a watch process starts
  • about every five minutes while it runs
  • at the end of a one-shot cctrace sync

No check starts for a run with --dry-run, --local, or --endpoint.

The check asks the server for a policy by sending the installation ID and the profile name; this request carries no upload token. The installation ID is a random UUID that cctrace creates in ~/.cctrace/installation-id on first use and that all profiles on the machine share. When the server has no policy for this client, nothing changes. Otherwise the client tests the policy's new addresses before applying it, and the test requests to the OTLP addresses carry the profile's upload token.

When a policy applies, the client writes the policy's certificate authority into the profile directory and rewrites the profile's server addresses, the Claude settings file in its Claude home, and, unless Codex sync is turned off for the profile, the Codex configuration file in the default Codex home, in the directory CODEX_HOME names when it is set, and in each directory of options.codex_dirs. A profile's explicit codex_home is handled on its own when Codex sync is on for the profile: the client moves the [otel] section there only if it is the section cctrace generates for the profile, keeping the token it carries, and otherwise leaves the file as it is without deferring the policy; see Server policy deferral. If the sync daemon is running, the client stops it and starts it again with the settings it ran with. A daemon started with --local or --endpoint cannot be moved this way: apply then changes nothing and ends with an error. Running Claude Code and Codex sessions use the new settings the next time they start.

A policy that would change a file another profile also uses is deferred instead of applied, unless it is a Codex configuration file and every profile that uses it moves to the same server; see Server policy deferral. After every run of cctrace config policy apply, the client reports the result to the server when the profile is logged in; see Privacy.

docs.title: Logs and state files
docs.text:
