Each profile keeps these files in its profile directory: ~/.cctrace/ for the default profile, ~/.cctrace/profiles/<name>/ for a named one.

File Contents ~/.cctrace/sync.log Daemon log. Rotates at 10 MB and keeps 5 old files. ~/.cctrace/sync-crash.log Raw output of the background process, such as panics. Trimmed when it passes 1 MB. ~/.cctrace/sync-state.json How far each Claude Code session file has been read ~/.cctrace/codex-sync-state.json, ~/.cctrace/gjc-sync-state.json, ~/.cctrace/omo-sync-state.json The same for Codex, GJC, and OMO ~/.cctrace/server-policy-state.json Server policy state: the last applied policy number, the latest status and reason, the last 32 results, and shared Codex configuration writes still waiting (path, digests of the old and new [otel] sections, old OTEL address and certificate path; no token) ~/.cctrace/sync.lock, ~/.cctrace/sync.pid, ~/.cctrace/sync-runtime.json Single-instance lock and the running daemon's pid and version

Keep the state files. A missing sync state file counts as a first run, so the next pass skips the existing content of every file instead of uploading it. A missing server policy state file makes the client forget which policy it applied, and the same policy can then fail to apply again; shared Codex configuration writes still waiting are dropped with it.

docs.title: Stop the daemon
docs.text:
cctrace sync --stop

--stop asks the daemon to finish and waits for it. It fails with no running daemon found when nothing is running. The next Claude Code session starts a new daemon through the hook.

If the daemon does not respond, force it:

cctrace kill

kill terminates the process holding the profile's sync lock, waits up to 5 seconds for the lock to be released, and clears the runtime files. When no daemon holds the lock it prints No running sync daemon and succeeds. It takes --profile and reads CCTRACE_PROFILE.

Both commands act on one profile. Add --profile <name> for a named one.

docs.title: Upgrading the client
docs.text:
Clients built from this repository without an update public key never replace themselves; for clients that do, see Security operations. A server built as described in Server install reports version dev, and the client then skips the update check. If the server reports a newer release version, the attempt fails because the client has an empty update public key, and ~/.cctrace/sync.log records the reason on an update: line, for example update: update public key is not configured. Collection continues on the current binary either way.

To upgrade:

  1. Rebuild the client (see Install) and copy it over the installed binary.
  2. If the new binary is at a different path, run cctrace env apply from it so that the hooks point at it.
  3. Restart the daemon so that it runs the new code: cctrace sync --stop, then cctrace sync --daemon or start a new Claude Code session.

While an older daemon is still running, cctrace status shows a notice under 수집 상태 naming both versions.

docs.title: Membership, upload exclusion, and collection execution
docs.text:
The multi-home profile change is under implementation and validation. Membership groups configuration; it is separate from upload permission and whether collection is running. A home allowed to upload still sends nothing while its profile collection is stopped. Usage monitoring remains independent.

Excluded accounts remain in the same list, last, with a gray/pale-red whole-card treatment and an explicit label. Both directions of Exclude session uploads require confirmation before saving. Neither direction moves profiles, starts collection, or changes usage monitoring.

Local upload permission cannot override server-enforced exclusions. Direct provider OTEL and session-file uploads are different paths; excluding session uploads does not by itself disable all telemetry.

docs.title: Reset and uninstall
docs.text:
cctrace reset removes a profile and its Claude Code wiring. cctrace uninstall removes every profile, the ~/.cctrace directory, and the binary.

Neither command deletes data already uploaded to the server.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Stop the sync daemon for each profile you are removing. Neither command stops a running daemon.

$ cctrace sync --stop
$ cctrace sync --stop --profile work

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
cctrace reset

Asks Remove default cctrace configuration? [y/N], then:

  1. Removes cctrace's entries from the default profile's Claude settings file (~/.claude/settings.json unless the profile names another Claude home):
    • the OTEL variables that cctrace manages under env, even if you had set any of them yourself;
    • the cctrace SessionStart and SessionEnd hooks, and any hook group or event left empty by that;
    • the cctrace stamp object.
  2. Deletes ~/.cctrace/profile.json.

Everything else under ~/.cctrace stays: the sync state files, the logs, and any named profiles. reset lists the named profiles that remain. Because the sync state is kept, running cctrace init again continues from where collection stopped.

Flag Effect --profile <name> Reset only this named profile: remove its entries from its Claude home's settings file and delete ~/.cctrace/profiles/<name>/, including that profile's sync state and log --all Reset the default profile and then every named profile --force Skip the confirmation prompt

reset does not change ~/.codex/config.toml. To stop Codex from sending metrics, delete the [otel] section from that file yourself. See Codex CLI.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
cctrace uninstall

Lists what it will do and asks Proceed? [y/N]. Only y continues. --force skips the prompt. Then it:

  1. Runs the equivalent of cctrace reset --all --force: cctrace's entries are removed from the settings file of every profile's Claude home, and every profile is deleted.
  2. Deletes the whole ~/.cctrace directory, including sync state and logs.
  3. Deletes every cctrace binary it finds in the directories on your PATH, in /usr/local/bin, and in ~/go/bin. Symbolic links are resolved to the file they point to. On macOS and Linux, a file it cannot delete is retried with sudo rm. On Windows, a binary that is in use is renamed and deleted a few seconds later.

A binary it cannot remove is reported with remove manually.

Note

uninstall deletes the sync state together with ~/.cctrace. If you install again later, the first sync treats the existing content of every session file as history and skips it.

Like reset, uninstall leaves the [otel] section in ~/.codex/config.toml in place.

docs.title: First admin
docs.text: Create the first administrator account at /setup with the setup token, then sign in at /login.

docs.title: Get the setup token
docs.text:
/setup accepts a request only with the setup token. The server decides the token when it starts:

Situation at startup Token The database has no dashboard users and CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN is set The value of CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN. It is not written to the log. The database has no dashboard users and CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN is empty A random token, printed once in the server log. A new one is generated at every start until the first admin exists. The database already has a user None. Setup is disabled.

The generated token appears on this line:

[cctraced] initial administrator setup token: <token>

With the Docker Compose stack from Install the server, read it with:

$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml logs cctraced

If the server cannot count users at startup, it logs [cctraced] setup disabled: user count failed: ... and refuses setup. Restart cctraced once the database is reachable.

docs.title: Create the account
docs.text:
1. Open the dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8080 on the server host, or your proxy address such as https://cctrace.company.example. While no user exists, the dashboard sends you to /setup.

  2. Fill in the form:

    Field Value Setup token The token from the previous section Email Your sign-in address, for example alice@example.com Name Display name Password, Confirm Password At least 8 characters

  3. Select Create Admin Account. The server creates the account with the admin role, signs you in, and opens the dashboard.

Once one user exists, /setup redirects to /login and the server answers further setup requests with setup already completed.

docs.title: If setup fails
docs.text:
Message Cause Setup token is invalid or setup is disabled. ... The server refused the request with HTTP 403. Usually the token is wrong, or it was generated by an earlier start. Read the latest token from the log. setup already completed A user already exists. Sign in at /login.

The page shows the token message for every HTTP 403, including a refusal by the browser-origin check. If the token is right, look for [api] CSRF rejected in the server log. The origin check compares the page's origin with the Host the server receives; a proxy that rewrites Host triggers it. See CCTRACE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS in Configuration.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Go to /login, enter your email and password, and select Sign In.

Message Cause invalid credentials Unknown email or wrong password account is disabled An administrator deactivated the account. See Users.

Signing in sets a 15-minute access cookie and a 7-day refresh cookie. The dashboard renews the access cookie with the refresh cookie; the refresh cookie itself is not renewed, so you sign in again 7 days after the last sign-in.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The account created at /setup has no team and no cctrace user ID, so it cannot pass cctrace init as it is. To send data from your own machine as this account, open its row menu on Users > Management, select Edit, and fill in Team and cctrace User ID. You can also add a separate account for yourself the same way as for anyone else: Users.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
What each dashboard page shows and who can use it.

Every page requires sign-in. A user account sees only its own sessions; aggregates are shared with every signed-in user. See Privacy.

Note

The screenshots on this page are a fictitious five-person team (Ivy, Marcus, Priya, Tomás, Yuki) on a demo server, not a real deployment.

docs.title: Header
docs.text: The header above every page holds an agent selector and an account selector. Pages that support them narrow their data to the selected agent and account. The account selector only appears when the signed-in account can see more than one account; a user account with no other account visible to it never sees the row.

docs.title: Overview (/)
docs.text:
The page you land on after sign-in.

Four summary cards report the trend chart's current range: Total Cost, Total Tokens, Active Users, Total Events. Total Cost carries a note that the figure is an estimate from API-priced usage, and that a subscription plan's own fee is prepaid separately from it.

Below the cards:

  • A filter bar: Cost/Token view, model category (All/Claude/Codex/Compatible), group by Model/by User, and model/user dropdown filters.
  • Cost Trend: a stacked area chart at Minute or Hourly granularity, and a stacked bar chart — one bar per bucket — at Daily, Weekly, or Monthly granularity. Date opens a custom since/until range. Unknown toggles a stacked segment for subscription burn the dashboard could not measure directly — an estimate from the gap between the provider's own usage meter and what OTEL/JSONL reported, with no user or model attribution; it is disabled when the range cannot support the estimate (a project, user, model, or agent filter is active, for example). Selecting a point on the chart narrows the cards and the panels below it to that point's range. A footnote states how much of the range's subscription burn the chart could measure, for example "Measured usage covers ≈100% of subscription burn over the last 7 days · readings span 100% of the range"; hover it for the method and, where eligible, each account's own fit.

  • Subscription burn (collapsible; labelled "preview" while collapsed): how much of each connected Claude/Codex subscription's quota window has been spent, per billing account. Toggle 5h/7d windows and Claude/Codex providers; Accounts draws one line per billing account, Weighted adds a price-weighted cross-account average (shown only once more than one priced account is on screen). The axis is inverted — 0% at the top, 100% consumed at the bottom — so a line's height is what is left of that window, and a reset reads as the line jumping back up. The headline reads "\<window> X% consumed · $Y of $Z left"; the footer states how many $/mo of subscription spend the chart could weight, and names any account it left out (an unpriced plan, or one with no reading in range).

Cost Trend switches from area to bar at Daily already, and stays bar through Weekly and Monthly. Subscription burn stays a step line until Weekly or Monthly, where it switches to one bar per bucket carrying a time-weighted average — because a step line would otherwise collapse into unreadable hatching across that many quota resets.

  • Cost by Model and Cost by User: the same range's totals from the two other angles, as a pie chart and a stacked bar.

docs.title: Usage (/cost)
docs.text:
The same Cost Trend chart as Overview, followed by the full per-user, per-model breakdown behind it: Requests, Input Tokens, Output Tokens, and Cost (or Total Tokens in Token view), sorted by cost and totalled in a footer row. The search box filters the table by user or model.

A row with no owner and the label weekly is not a person — it is the tokens the server's own Codex account spent building the weekly AI report; hover it for the explanation.

docs.title: Users (/users)
docs.text: The Analytics tab lists users by cost. Selecting a person's card opens an inline Detail View next to it. Administrators also get the Management tab, described in Users.

docs.title: Sessions (/sessions)
docs.text:
A session list on the left and the selected session's transcript on the right.

  • Select a session in the list to open its transcript. The list loads more as you scroll and shows how many sessions match out of the total.
  • Assembled merges related session files (subagents, branches) into one conversation. Raw shows each file's records as they are, grouped by file.
  • Interactive (the default) shows sessions with human turns, Headless shows machine-driven sessions such as claude -p, All shows both.
  • The project picker narrows the list to one project. The search box filters the loaded sessions by session, user, or project.

A transcript's tool calls render for what the recording agent actually sent: a Claude session's Read/Edit/Bash steps —

— and a Codex session's apply_patch/shell steps, filtered here to sessions tagged codex with the Agent selector:

docs.title: Delete a session
docs.text:
The trash icon in the transcript header (tooltip 세션 삭제) deletes the session's records and the events and metrics attached to it. This cannot be undone, and the server refuses the session if a client uploads it again.

Who Can delete admin Any session. The dialog then offers to delete the project's other sessions and to stop collecting the project. user Their own sessions, while the owner-delete policy allows it (the default)

Administrators set the owner-delete policy and remove projects from the blocked list in the gear dialog next to the trash icon (세션 수집 설정). They can also delete a whole project from the project picker.

docs.title: A user account's own sessions
docs.text: A user account's /sessions is the same list-and-transcript page, narrowed to its own sessions with no Account selector (and no Admin entry in the sidebar):

docs.title: Weekly report (/weekly)
docs.text:
A signed-in account's own record for one calendar week, navigated with the arrows next to the week label; a week in progress is marked so, and a week that has not started yet is not reachable.

The summary line under the title counts that week's sessions by agent and its rule-derived "work segments" (Claude Code 세션 N · Codex 세션 N · 작업 구간 N); it also carries any caveats that apply that week, for example the same OTEL-metric scope note used on the Tools page for Codex tool counts, records an administrator excluded from analysis, or sessions not covered by a work-segment fact.

  • Projects: a donut of that week's sessions by project.
  • Task types: the week's turns grouped by task type; selecting a type opens its underlying session segments. A dataset with no classification run yet shows every turn as Not yet classified.
  • The AI report panel reads the week's task segments' conversation content and writes a summary and a to-revisit list — off by default, and shown as "AI 리포트가 꺼져 있습니다" until an administrator turns it on.

docs.title: Tools (/tools)
docs.text:
Claude Code and Codex tool calls over the last 30 days: total uses, successes, failures, and the overall success rate, then a per-tool table with a success-rate bar.

A scope note under the title states what the Codex figures rest on: Codex's tool counts come from its codex.tool.call OTEL metric, which counts calls made inside a code-mode exec script and is sent only by TUI and VS Code runs; Codex also carries no per-call failure detail, so a tool's expandable Recent Failures list is Claude's calls only.

docs.title: Plugins & Skills (/plugins)
docs.text:
Calls to Claude Code slash commands and skills, and Codex skill injections, grouped by plugin or skill name.

  • Period: 7d, 30d (default), 90d, All.
  • Summary cards: Claude Calls, Codex Calls, Avg Tokens, Total, Input, Output tokens.
  • Views: By Skill, By User, By Project. By Project counts only sessions in git repositories.

/skills redirects here.

docs.title: Rules (/rules)
docs.text:
The CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files the client found in the git repositories your sessions ran in, with their version history.

  • Filter by text, status (Active, Missing), and repository. Summary cards count Repositories and Rule Files.
  • Select a file to read a version and add comments to it.
  • A user account sees rule files only from repositories where it has sessions.

docs.title: Logs (/logs)
docs.text:
Raw telemetry from the last 30 days, 50 rows per page.

Tab Columns Events Time, Event, Model, Session, User, Input, Output, Cost, Age Metrics Time, Metric, Model, User, Value, Session, Age

Logs are not limited to your own data. Attributes that carry free text, such as prompts and tool output, are removed before they reach the page.

docs.title: Admin (/admin)
docs.text:
Visible only to administrators.

Tab Shows Clients Each client that reported a version: Profile Email, Name, User ID, Client Version, Last Seen, Status Storage Retention, table sizes, and free space on the data volume. Retention is edited here; see Operations.

/versions and /storage redirect to /admin.

The Excluded Accounts, Unpriced Models, Insights, and AI tabs are under active development and are not documented here.

docs.title: Settings (/settings)
docs.text:
• Change Password: enter the current password and a new one of at least 8 characters. An account with a temporary password is sent here until it changes it.
  • Appearance: accent color, agent tone, and whether the logo mark is shown.

The API token and billing account sections are under active development and are not documented here.

docs.title: Pages under active development
docs.text:
These pages exist and are under active development. They are not documented here.

Page Sidebar entry /open-api Open API

docs.title: Users
docs.text: Administrators create one dashboard account per person. The account's cctrace user ID is what ties the data a client sends to that person.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Sees and does admin Every user's sessions, the Management tab on /users, the /admin page, project deletion user Their own sessions; the aggregates every signed-in user shares

What each role can read is detailed in Privacy.

docs.title: Add a user
docs.text:
1. Open Users (/users) and select the Management tab. Only administrators see it.

  2. Select Add User and fill in every field. The server rejects the request if any is empty.

    Field Value Email The person's sign-in address, for example alice@example.com Name Display name Role User or Admin Team Team name. cctrace init fails if the account has no team. The admin created at /setup has no team until one is set with Edit. cctrace User ID A short identifier, for example alice. The person enters it in cctrace init. The field suggests user IDs already seen in received telemetry.

  3. The dialog shows a Temporary Password once. Give it to the person together with the cctrace user ID.

Error Cause email already exists Another account has this email cctrace_user_id already assigned to another user Another account has this user ID

docs.title: First sign-in of a new user
docs.text:
1. The person signs in at /login with the email and the temporary password.

  2. Until the password is changed, the dashboard sends every page to /settings and the other navigation entries are disabled.

  3. The person sets a new password (at least 8 characters) under Change Password.

The server refuses cctrace init authentication while a temporary password is pending; init stops with please change your password on the dashboard before authenticating. After the change, continue with Connect.

docs.title: How data is attributed to an account
docs.text:
• cctrace init authenticates with the cctrace user ID and password. The server returns the account's name, email, and team, and an upload token. The client stores them in its profile.
  • Every session upload carries the profile's user ID and email.
  • The OTEL environment that init writes labels telemetry with the user ID, name, email, and team through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES (user.id=<id>,user.name=<name>,user.profile.email=<email>,user.team=<team>). When telemetry arrives with a user's upload token, the server attributes it to the account that owns the token.
  • The dashboard shows a user account the data stored under its cctrace user ID. An account without one (the not set badge in the list) sees no session data (with the default CCTRACE_USERID_ACCESS_CONTROL).
  • Changing an account's cctrace user ID does not move data already stored under the old ID.

docs.title: Manage accounts
docs.text:
Open the row menu on the Management tab.

Action Effect Edit Change name, team, role, or cctrace user ID. A team that is set cannot be emptied: Save is disabled with Team is required. Deactivate / Activate A deactivated account cannot sign in (account is disabled), cannot authenticate cctrace init, and its upload token is refused, so its clients stop sending data. Stored data is kept. Reset Password Issues a new temporary password, shown once. At the next sign-in the person must change it again, and cctrace init is refused until then. Collection with the existing upload token continues. Revoke API Token Shown when the account has a token. Deletes all of the account's tokens, including the upload token. The person's clients stop sending data until they run cctrace init again. Clear Collected Data Deletes the telemetry, session logs, live state, policy target reports, client version record, latest usage-limit reading and privacy settings stored under the account's email. What stays is listed under Delete data. This cannot be undone.

There is no action that deletes an account; deactivate it instead.

Role and deactivation changes reach an open browser session within 15 minutes: the dashboard's access cookie lasts 15 minutes, and renewing it reads the account again.

docs.title: Analytics tab
docs.text: The Analytics tab of /users, visible to every signed-in user, lists users ordered by cost. The cost figures are under active development and are not documented here.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text: Commands of the cctrace client that are covered by this guide. cctrace --help and cctrace <command> --help list every flag.

docs.title: Setup and configuration
docs.text:
Command Flags Does cctrace init --profile <name> Authenticate against the server, write the profile and the agent settings. See Connect. cctrace status --profile <name> Show identity, endpoints, collection state, paths, options, and quota. Exit code 1 without a profile, 2 when the OTEL endpoint is unreachable. cctrace env apply --profile <name>, --all Rewrite the OTEL variables and hooks in the Claude settings file from the saved profile, using the current binary's path cctrace config list --profile <name> List profile settings, tokens masked. cctrace config alone does the same. cctrace config get <key> --profile <name> Print one setting cctrace config set <key> <value> --profile <name> Change one setting and rewrite the Claude settings file. Keys are listed in Connect. cctrace config policy status --profile <name> Print the installation ID, the profile name, and the profile's server policy state as JSON. Contacts no server. cctrace config policy check --profile <name> Fetch the server's signed policy, verify it, probe its new addresses, and print the policy with the files an apply would change (when no policy applies, or it is already applied, it prints the same state as status). Writes no settings and no policy state. Needs an update public key or a policy public key. cctrace config policy apply --profile <name> Fetch, verify, and apply the server's signed policy, then report the result to the server if the profile is logged in. Needs an update public key or a policy public key.

config policy works with the signed server policy described in Sync daemon. check and apply verify it with the update public key or the policy public key linked into the client. A client built from this repository without an update or policy public key has neither, so both end with policy public key is not configured; rebuild with main.policyPublicKeyBase64 or main.updatePublicKeyBase64, while status still works. apply reports that failure to the server too when the profile is logged in. The installation ID is a random UUID in ~/.cctrace/installation-id; whichever of status, check, and apply runs first creates it. What a report contains is listed in Privacy.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Command Flags Does cctrace profile add <name> --home <dir> (required) Copy the default profile into a named profile for another Claude home and wire that home cctrace profile list List named profiles and their Claude homes cctrace profile edit <name> --home <dir>, --codex-home <dir> Change the Claude home or Codex home of a named profile without rewriting any settings file. Run cctrace env apply --profile <name> afterwards to write the OTEL variables and hooks into a new Claude home. cctrace profile remove <name> --force Delete a named profile's directory. Leaves its Claude settings entries; use cctrace reset --profile to remove those too. cctrace profile claim <name> --source <id\|folder> (repeatable), --all, --force Give the profile a source it shares with another profile, which the other profile lets go of first. Needs the local daemon running; asks for confirmation unless --force.

See Profiles.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
Command Does cctrace sync One pass for the default profile and every named profile cctrace sync --daemon Start the background daemon for one profile cctrace sync --stop Stop the daemon gracefully cctrace sync status Print what the running daemon last published as a table: profiles and the sources held back from them. --json prints the raw snapshot. cctrace kill Force-terminate the daemon holding the profile's sync lock. Takes --profile. Flag Default Meaning --watch off Run in the foreground and keep polling --interval <duration> 30s Poll interval for watch mode --daemon off Run in the background --once off With --daemon: one pass, then exit --stop off Stop the running daemon --dry-run off Show what would be sent without sending --claude-dir <dir> profile's Claude home Claude config directory to read --profile <name> CCTRACE_PROFILE Named profile --auto-profile off Pick the profile whose Claude home matches --claude-dir or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR --profile-email <email> CCTRACE_PROFILE_EMAIL Override the email attached to records --endpoint <url> profile's sync endpoint Override the upload endpoint --local off Development use: send to a server on localhost

See Sync daemon for details.

docs.title: Local analysis
docs.text:
Commands that serve this machine's session logs to the dashboard in your browser. Serving uploads nothing; with local enable, the sync daemon still uploads as the profile's options say. See Local analysis.

Command Flags Does cctrace local serve --origin (required), --address, --claude-dir, --codex-dir Serve the local session API on a loopback address in the foreground until you stop it. Prints the endpoint and a new random token as JSON. The token is not stored. cctrace local enable --origin (required), --profile <name> Allow the profile's sync daemon to serve the local session API for that origin on a fixed loopback port. Prints the endpoint and a token once; only a hash of the token is kept. Running it again issues a new token and picks a new port. cctrace local status --profile <name> Print as JSON whether local analysis is enabled and running, with its origin and address cctrace local disable --profile <name> Revoke the token and turn local analysis off for the profile. A daemon that is serving stops serving. Flag of local serve Default Meaning --origin <origin> required Web origin allowed to call the API. Repeatable. --address <ip:port> 127.0.0.1:0 Loopback IP address and port to listen on. Port 0 picks a free port. --claude-dir <dir> see below Claude config directory to read. Repeatable. --codex-dir <dir> see below Codex home to read. Repeatable.

With neither --claude-dir nor --codex-dir, local serve reads the default Claude home, the default Codex home and CODEX_HOME, and the Claude and Codex homes configured for each profile. With either flag, it reads only the directories given.

docs.title: Removal
docs.text:
Command Flags Does cctrace reset --profile <name>, --all, --force Remove a profile and its Claude settings entries. Sync state is kept for the default profile. cctrace uninstall --force Reset every profile, delete ~/.cctrace, and delete the cctrace binaries on PATH

See Reset and uninstall.

docs.title: Environment variables read by the client
docs.text: Variable Used by Effect CCTRACE_PROFILE sync, kill, config policy Named profile when --profile is not given CCTRACE_PROFILE_EMAIL sync Email attached to records when --profile-email is not given CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR sync --auto-profile Claude home to match when --claude-dir is not given CODEX_CONFIG_DIR init, sync Codex home in place of ~/.codex CODEX_HOME sync Additional Codex home to scan CCTRACE_CODEX_SYNC, CCTRACE_GJC_SYNC, CCTRACE_OMO_SYNC sync true enables that agent's collection regardless of the profile option

docs.title: Other commands
docs.text: Read and analysis commands exist but are under active development and are not documented here: report, usage, ls, events, projects, sessions, tools, plugins, skills, rules, organization-insights, insights, backfill-quota, and auth read.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Every port the server stack publishes, from deploy/docker-compose.yml and the optional deploy/docker-compose.tls.yml.

Host bind addresses and host ports are set in the server env file (.env in the deploy/ directory). See Configuration.

docs.title: Base stack
docs.text:
Service Container port Host bind (default) Host port (default) Protocol Purpose cctraced 8080 HTTP_BIND (127.0.0.1) HTTP_PORT (8080) HTTP Dashboard, REST API, client sync cctraced 4317 GRPC_BIND (0.0.0.0) GRPC_PORT (4317) OTLP over gRPC Telemetry ingest cctraced 4318 OTEL_HTTP_BIND (0.0.0.0) OTEL_HTTP_PORT (4318) OTLP over HTTP Telemetry ingest timescaledb 5432 127.0.0.1 (fixed) DB_PORT (5432) PostgreSQL Database

None of these ports use TLS.

Warning

With the defaults, OTLP on 4317 and 4318 is reachable on every host interface in plaintext. Restrict it with the bind settings, a firewall or VPN, or the TLS overlay below.

docs.title: TLS overlay
docs.text:
Added by deploy/docker-compose.tls.yml. Caddy terminates TLS and forwards to cctraced over the compose network.

Service Container port Host bind (default) Host port (default) Forwards to Purpose caddy 8443 TLS_BIND (0.0.0.0) TLS_HTTP_PORT (8443) cctraced 8080 Dashboard, REST API, client sync over HTTPS caddy 5317 TLS_BIND (0.0.0.0) TLS_GRPC_PORT (5317) cctraced 4317 OTLP over gRPC with TLS caddy 5318 TLS_BIND (0.0.0.0) TLS_OTEL_HTTP_PORT (5318) cctraced 4318 OTLP over HTTP with TLS

When you use the overlay, set HTTP_BIND, GRPC_BIND and OTEL_HTTP_BIND to 127.0.0.1 so the plaintext ports are not reachable beside the TLS ones. See Install.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
What cctrace collects, where it keeps it, who can read it, and how long it stays.

The server stores conversation content

Session logs include what people typed, the agent's replies, and tool commands and output. By default they are kept until an operator sets a retention period. Decide on retention and redaction before you connect other people.

docs.title: What is collected
docs.text:
Data Sent by Contents OTEL telemetry The agent itself, to the OTLP ports Metrics and events: token counts, cost, model, tool activity. cctrace init labels them with the user ID, name, email, and team through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. Session logs The sync daemon, to /api/sync Each line of the agent's session files as written on disk: prompts, replies, reasoning text, tool calls with their arguments and output. Each upload also carries project details: directory name, git remote URL, repository name, branch, and commit. Session snapshots and the collector heartbeat The sync daemon, to /api/session-observations For each Claude Code session, from its metadata lines: the AI title, the custom title and the agent name; the cost total and the lines added and removed of each run; the model ids used; the PR links it recorded; and the ids of the sessions it continued in. Also counts of the files the session edited: how many there are, how many git status still reports as uncommitted, how many repositories they lie in, how many git could not place, when the counts last changed, and whether they miss edits the client never read; never the paths. Also verified git-call commit identities and optional subjects, with unresolved call reasons (described below). For each Codex session, from its rollout file, each turn's id and the id of the turn it belongs under, when it started and ended, whether it completed, was aborted (with the reason Codex gives) or ended in an error (with the error's kind, never its message), its duration and time to first token, the model context window, the collaboration mode, the model and the reasoning effort. With them, a heartbeat saying the collector is running. Live session status and session ends The sync daemon, to /api/session-observations For each running Claude Code session process, read about once a minute from the state file Claude Code keeps for it (~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json): the session's status (busy, idle, waiting, shell, or gone once the process has ended), what a waiting session waits for (input, permission, dialog, sandbox, worker, goal or other), the session's name and where the name came from, the process id and start time, when the status last changed, and the session's project. When a session ends, the reason the SessionEnd hook gives, such as clear or logout, and the session's project. The project is the session's project directory name, which spells out the path of its working directory. On Windows Claude Code writes no procStart to the state file, so no live status is sent from Windows. Rule files The sync daemon The CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files at the root of the git repositories your sessions run in Usage-limit readings The client The plan's rate-limit usage as read on your machine Policy request The client, to /api/client-config-policy Asked by each policy check: the installation ID (a random UUID that cctrace creates under ~/.cctrace the first time a policy command runs) and the profile name, as query parameters, with no token. The server answers from its policy file and stores nothing from the request. Its access log keeps the method, path, status, duration and the caller's address, not the query. Policy target report The client, to /api/client-policy-report For a profile that is logged in, one record after each cctrace config policy apply run, whatever the run found: the installation ID and profile name (empty for the default profile), the email attached to the profile's uploaded records and the user ID, the server and OTLP addresses the profile uses and its OTLP protocol, the number of the last policy it applied, how the run ended (ok, deferred or failed), the number of the policy a failed or deferred run had reached, and the client's own error text. The error text can name local file paths and other profiles, and is cut to 500 characters; a path of a profile's explicit Codex home is replaced by [explicit Codex home]. An ok run can carry text too, until the next policy: when a policy leaves the default Codex configuration as it found it, the text names that file's absolute local path, and when it leaves an explicit Codex home's configuration as it found it, the text is explicit Codex home kept, with no path. The request headers add the client version, OS and architecture; the server stores only the version. Client version record The client, with each /api/sync upload For each account email: the user ID, the version, OS and architecture from the request headers, the time of the last sync and, for a client that reports it, its self-update state: the version it fails to reach, the number of consecutive failures, the times of the first and last failure, and the error text (it can name local file paths and is cut to 500 characters). Account exclusion and options.collect_repository_prefixes do not stop it.

cctrace init does not set OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, so Claude Code's own telemetry does not carry prompt text unless you set that variable yourself. Session logs carry the full conversation either way.

A session snapshot is attributed to the billing account of the newest record the client has read from that session. If the account changes partway through a session, the whole snapshot goes under the newer account, and an account exclusion is judged by that account. A Codex session's snapshot goes under the account signed in to the Codex home its rollout file is in, as of the newest turn line the client has read, and is sent only by a sync that reads that Codex home.

To count a session's uncommitted files, the client finds on your machine the repository each file the session edited with Edit, Write, MultiEdit or NotebookEdit lies in, by the nearest .git above it, checks with git rev-parse where git puts that repository's work tree, and runs git status there, asking about those files alone. It keeps those file paths in its sync state, counts again about once an hour while the session has been active in the last seven days, sends the counts when they change, and once those seven days have passed drops the paths and keeps the last counts. With options.collect_repository_prefixes set, it reads each such repository's origin to judge it, git status runs only in the repositories it collects, and a file in any other repository, or in none, is not counted. No git runs for a session whose account is excluded. Codex sessions get no such counts.

A live status is attributed to the account signed in to that Claude home when the status is read, and a session end to the one signed in when the session ended. Neither is sent for an excluded account or for a repository outside options.collect_repository_prefixes. The SessionEnd hook's transcript path and working directory stay on your machine; only the project they belong to is sent. Until a sync sends it, a session end waits in a pending directory beside the profile's sync state (~/.cctrace/pending/ for the default profile), for at most seven days.

For Claude Code git calls, the client also reads up to 2,000 entries of the allowed work tree's HEAD reflog and its current branch. Only a creation candidate named by that call's output hash is attached to the snapshot: full hash, commit time, parent count, kind, repository, recent branch, call id, transcript identifier, proof, optional amend predecessor, and a subject of at most 200 bytes. Time or a matching subject alone is not proof. Unresolved calls carry only their id, transcript identifier, time and reason. Commit items and unresolved calls each have a 100-entry limit within the snapshot's 60 KiB limit; lost coverage is marked truncated. Commands, output text and unverified candidate subjects are not saved in the call state. Pending calls keep directories and hash evidence locally, and expire after seven days with an unresolved reason. Commit lookup uses at most 2.5 seconds of the same five-second flush budget used for uncommitted counts. Excluded accounts and repositories are not inspected for commit subjects.

The policy request and the policy target report belong to signed server policies, which only a client that links an update public key or a policy public key can use. Builds from this repository without an update or policy public key link empty keys (see Overview). Such a client never starts the background policy check and never sends a policy request. cctrace config policy apply ends with an error that begins "policy public key is not configured" and, for a profile that is logged in, still sends one report of that failed run each time you run it. A client that does link a key runs the background check when a watch process starts, about every five minutes while it runs, and at the end of a one-shot cctrace sync; each run ends with a report from a profile that is logged in. A profile that is not logged in sends no report, and neither do cctrace config policy status and cctrace config policy check.

docs.title: Where it is stored
docs.text:
Collected data goes to the server you configured and into its TimescaleDB database. Other outbound requests:

  • To read usage limits, the client queries Anthropic's usage API with the local Claude Code login.
  • The server downloads OpenAI's public pricing and changelog pages to price Codex usage.
  • A client that links an update public key or a policy public key tests a policy it received before applying it (cctrace config policy check and apply): small requests to the policy's new server and OTLP addresses, where the OTLP requests carry the profile's upload token.

A policy target report is kept as one row per installation ID and profile: a new report replaces the row's values and keeps the time the row was first seen, and an empty version header does not erase the version stored before. A client version record is kept as one row per account email, updated by each sync. The server checks the form of a report, not whether it is true: a logged-in client can report any installation ID and profile. A report with a malformed or too long field is refused with HTTP 400 and the reason is logged (see Operations).

The weekly AI report feature, when enabled, sends data to the AI provider it is configured with. It is under active development and is not documented here.

Clients warn, but do not refuse, when an endpoint is plain http:// to anything but the same machine (loopback), private addresses included. Put the server behind TLS before clients connect over a network you do not control; see Install the server.

docs.title: Who can see what
docs.text:
Data admin user Session transcripts (/sessions) Every user's Their own Rule files (/rules) All repositories Repositories where they have sessions Aggregates: usage, cost, tools, plugins and skills, per-user lists Everyone's Everyone's Telemetry rows (/logs) Everyone's Everyone's User management, /admin Yes No
  • Aggregates are shared on purpose, so the whole team's usage adds up in one place.
  • Attributes that carry free text (prompts, tool arguments and output, command text, stdout and stderr) are removed from telemetry rows before any dashboard response, for administrators too. They may still be stored.
  • A user account sees its own sessions through its cctrace user ID. An account without one sees no session data (with the default CCTRACE_USERID_ACCESS_CONTROL). See Users.
  • Client version records are shown to administrators only, on the Clients tab of /admin.
  • Policy target reports have no dashboard page and no API that reads them. They can be read only in the database.

docs.title: CCTRACE_USERID_ACCESS_CONTROL
docs.text:
Value How a user account's sessions are matched unset or anything but false (default) By the account's cctrace user ID false By the account's sign-in email against the email the client uploaded with

The setting changes only how sessions are matched to their owner. It does not make aggregates private.

docs.title: Redact on the client
docs.text:
Two profile options remove content from session logs before they leave your machine. Both are off by default.

cctrace config set options.redact_user_prompts true
cctrace config set options.redact_tool_details true
Option Replaces the values of these fields redact_user_prompts content, text, thinking, summary, title redact_tool_details arguments, input, output, result, command, description, stdout, stderr
  • Values are replaced with [redacted by cctrace client], wherever the field appears in the record. A line that cannot be parsed is replaced as a whole.
  • Token counts, cost, model, and timestamps are left alone, so dashboard figures do not change.
  • Redaction covers session logs, the titles in session snapshots and the session names in live status. It does not touch OTEL telemetry, which the agent sends directly, rule files, policy target reports or client version records.
  • It applies to uploads made after the change. Records already on the server keep what they hold; re-enrichment can add fields to them.
  • A running sync daemon keeps the options it started with. Restart it with cctrace sync --stop and then cctrace sync --daemon.

Some content in Claude Code session lines sits under names that also mean something else, so it is found by line kind and position rather than by field name. Each kind of content in this table gets the same treatment in every place the table names:

Content redact_user_prompts redact_tool_details Questions and options asked through AskUserQuestion, and the plan ExitPlanMode presents (tool input) Hidden Hidden Answers to AskUserQuestion (the answers field of toolUseResult, and annotations) Hidden Hidden Tool output inside tool_result blocks (content) Hidden Hidden A prompt typed while the agent was busy (queued_command attachment, prompt) Hidden Kept A background task's result: queued (queued_command with commandMode task-notification) and as its own user line (an origin of kind task-notification, the content of message) Hidden Hidden Plan file text (plan_file_reference, planContent) Hidden Hidden Plan file paths (plan_file_reference and plan_mode, planFilePath) Kept Hidden Task subjects (task_reminder attachment, content) Hidden Hidden Claude Code's recap (system line with subtype away_summary, content) Hidden Hidden The summary a session continued after compaction opens with (user line with isCompactSummary, the content of message) Hidden Hidden Verified commit subjects in session snapshots Hidden; subjects read while either option is on stay hidden after it is turned off Hidden; also applied again when sending Session titles and agent names in session snapshots (/api/session-observations) Hidden; a title first read while the option was on stays hidden after it is turned off Kept Session names in live session status (/api/session-observations) Hidden; unlike a title, a name is read afresh every minute and goes as the option says when it is sent, so once the option is turned off a session's current name goes in plain text Kept

Fields that record what happened rather than what was said, such as prompt ids, permission mode, turn durations and counts, task status, and the model in use, are not redacted. Neither option hides commit hashes, times, kinds, parent counts, repositories, branches, call identifiers or unresolved reasons, or the PR links, cost and line totals, model ids, continued-in session ids, edited and uncommitted file counts, or Codex turn times, endings and error kinds, models and efforts in session snapshots, nor a live session's status, what it waits for, its process id and start time, or the reason a session ended.

With redact_tool_details alone, some tool output stays, because Claude Code writes it into a user line as conversation text rather than under a tool field. These gaps are older than the rules above; redact_user_prompts removes all of them:

  • The tool results an SDK harness writes as text, such as Tool result (Bash, id=…)
  • The output of a ! shell command (<bash-stdout>)
  • The output of a local slash command (<local-command-stdout>)

Add --profile <name> to act on a named profile. cctrace status lists the redaction that is on.

docs.title: Re-enrichment
docs.text:
cctrace sync reenrich reads session files again from the start and adds the fields a newer client collects to records already on the server. It runs only when you type it.

  • It sends only the fields it can add, never the conversation itself (message). By default those are the fields that record what happened. Answers, queued prompts and background task results, plan files and their paths, task subjects, and recaps stay on your machine.
  • --include-content sends and adds those too, under the redaction options in force when you run it. A record collected while redaction was on, before these fields were collected, gains them in plain text if redaction is now off. The command says so before it sends anything.
  • A value a record already holds is never replaced, a [redacted by cctrace client] marker included. Conversation text is never added or changed.
  • It leaves alone the part of a file that was already on disk when sync first ran, which sync never collected. For a file sync once found shrunk, it also leaves alone everything before the size the file had then. That part can include lines sync did collect, so those records are not re-enriched.
  • Lines sync consumed without collecting them, because their repository was outside options.collect_repository_prefixes, are left alone too, together with everything before them; the session snapshot rebuild skips the same part. As a side effect, narrowing the allowlist and widening it again leaves out of re-enrichment the lines collected before it was narrowed.
  • It also builds each session's snapshot (see What is collected) from the same part of the file, and sends the snapshots before it exits. By default the snapshot leaves out the titles and the agent name; --include-content includes them, under the redaction options in force then. A snapshot without titles does not take the place of one this client has sent with titles.
  • With Codex sync on, it builds each Codex session's turns the same way, from the part of its rollout file sync collected, and sends them in the same flush.

  • For a session active in the last seven days, it also reads from the same part the files the session edited, so its uncommitted count covers the whole session rather than what was read since this client. The paths stay on your machine.

  • Git call backfill uses that same collected portion without a seven-day age cutoff. By default verified commits omit the subject key; --include-content permits subjects under both current redaction policies. A subject or redaction marker already present is not replaced by re-enrichment.

docs.title: Local analysis
docs.text:
cctrace local serve, and the local service that cctrace local enable turns on, read the Claude Code and Codex session files on your machine and show them in the dashboard without a sync. See Local analysis.

  • The service listens only on a loopback address, refuses browser requests from any origin you did not name, and serves session data only to requests that carry its token.
  • It makes no outbound request. The dashboard page reads it directly from your browser, without cookies, so this path sends nothing to the server.
  • serve makes a new token on each run and prints it once. enable prints the token once and keeps only its SHA-256 hash, in the profile's directory under ~/.cctrace. disable discards the hash.
  • If you choose "이 탭에 연결 저장" (remember the connection in this tab) when you connect, the browser keeps the service address and the token in sessionStorage until the tab closes. The dashboard page never writes the token to its address, to a server request or to a log.

docs.title: Delete data
docs.text:
What Who How One session Its owner (while the owner-delete policy allows it) or an administrator Trash icon on /sessions. See Pages. A project's sessions, and future collection of it Administrator Session delete dialog or the project picker on /sessions Telemetry, session logs, live state, policy target reports, the client version record, the latest usage-limit reading and the settings that hide the account's sessions from AI session records (the overview, review items, work status and tags an AI model writes for each session), stored under one account's email (the rows named below the table stay) Administrator Clear Collected Data on /users. See Users.

A deleted session is refused if a client uploads it again.

Merging accounts moves an account's policy target reports and its client version record to the account it is merged into. When both accounts have a client version record, the two are combined the way a sync updates one: the record synced last wins, but where it lacks the version, OS, architecture or self-update state, the other record's is kept. The settings that hide the account's sessions from AI session records move too, and the target account sees them as its own. Settings saved under a cctrace user ID stay where they are and keep applying through that ID. Where the target already has the same setting, the target's stays. A moved setting that covers the whole account hides the target account's own sessions as well. The account's latest usage-limit reading is deleted, not moved: the target's own reports keep its reading current.

Clear Collected Data also deletes the settings that hide the account's sessions from AI session records. Sessions collected for the account afterwards are therefore no longer hidden from them until the settings are set again through /api/privacy.

Neither Clear Collected Data nor merging accounts removes rule file versions, which record the account's email as their author. Nor do they remove or move the history of the account's usage-limit readings (quota_samples) and the list of excluded addresses derived from it, or the hourly usage aggregates older than 48 hours that name it. Those rows can stay in the database until an operator deletes them there.

A merge leaves one latest usage-limit reading for both profiles. If they were signed in to different Claude accounts, their later reports are stored under the target's address and replace each other in turn. The history of readings does not follow the merge: each reading keeps the name of the profile that reported it.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
Table Contents Default otel_events Telemetry events Dropped after 90 days, compressed after 30 otel_metrics Telemetry metrics Dropped after 90 days, compressed after 30 session_records Session logs (conversation content) No policy: kept until an operator sets one client_policy_reports Policy target reports Not covered by retention settings: kept until Clear Collected Data or an operator deletes the rows client_versions Client version records Not covered by retention settings: kept until Clear Collected Data or an operator deletes the rows

While session_records has no policy, the server logs this at startup:

[cctraced] notice: session_records (conversation content) has no retention policy and is kept indefinitely, while otel_events/otel_metrics are dropped after 90 days. Set SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS (0 = keep forever) or choose an interval in Admin -> Storage.

Set retention on the Storage tab of /admin. cctraced also reads SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS and OTEL_RETENTION_DAYS, but the shipped compose file does not pass them to the container (Configuration). When one reaches the container, it wins and locks that setting in the dashboard. Shortening retention deletes existing data. Details: Operations.

docs.title: Server environment
docs.text:
Every server setting covered by this guide, in one table. Details and caveats are in Configuration.

"Where set" means:

  • env file: set in the server env file (.env in the deploy/ directory) and used by deploy/docker-compose.yml.
  • env file, TLS: read only when deploy/docker-compose.tls.yml is used.
  • compose (fixed): set by the compose file itself; not meant to be changed.
  • not passed: read by cctraced, but the shipped compose file does not pass it to the container.
Name Where set Default Meaning JWT_SECRET env file none (required) Dashboard session signing key, at least 32 bytes LOGS_DIR env file none (required) Host directory mounted at /data/logs for the access log DB_PASSWORD env file cctrace Database superuser password, applied at first initialisation only DB_APP_CREDENTIALS env file empty <user>:<password> of the non-superuser role cctraced connects as, created at first initialisation only; empty connects as the superuser DB_PORT env file 5432 Host port for TimescaleDB, bound to 127.0.0.1 HTTP_BIND env file 127.0.0.1 Host address for the dashboard and REST API GRPC_BIND env file 0.0.0.0 Host address for OTLP gRPC OTEL_HTTP_BIND env file 0.0.0.0 Host address for OTLP HTTP HTTP_PORT env file 8080 Host port for the dashboard and REST API GRPC_PORT env file 4317 Host port for OTLP gRPC OTEL_HTTP_PORT env file 4318 Host port for OTLP HTTP IMAGE_TAG env file latest Local tag of cctrace/cctraced DB_IMAGE_TAG env file latest Local tag of cctrace/timescaledb-pgmq CONTAINER_PREFIX env file cctrace Container name prefix CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN env file empty (generated and logged) First-admin token; invalid after the first admin exists COOKIE_SECURE env file 0 1 forces Secure auth cookies CCTRACE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS env file empty (CORS off) Comma-separated exact browser origins API_KEY env file empty Optional shared API token CCTRACE_SERVER_POLICY_FILE env file empty (no policy served) Path of a signed server policy file, as the cctraced container sees it. Read on every request; see Operations CCTRACE_MAX_SYNC_BODY_BYTES env file 8388608 Maximum POST /api/sync body in bytes, up to 268435456 CADDY_SITE_ADDRESS env file, TLS none (required by the overlay) Hostname or IP address clients use CADDY_TLS_MODE env file, TLS internal internal (Caddy's own CA) or acme TLS_BIND env file, TLS 0.0.0.0 Host address for the TLS ports TLS_HTTP_PORT env file, TLS 8443 Host port for HTTPS TLS_GRPC_PORT env file, TLS 5317 Host port for OTLP gRPC with TLS TLS_OTEL_HTTP_PORT env file, TLS 5318 Host port for OTLP HTTP with TLS DATABASE_URL compose (fixed) built from DB_APP_CREDENTIALS / DB_PASSWORD Database connection string HTTP_PORT (container) compose (fixed) 8080 Port cctraced listens on for HTTP GRPC_PORT (container) compose (fixed) 4317 Port cctraced listens on for OTLP gRPC HTTP_OTEL_PORT compose (fixed) 4318 Port cctraced listens on for OTLP HTTP WAL_DIR compose (fixed) /data/buffer-wal Ingest spill directory, on the wal_data volume OTEL_RETENTION_DAYS not passed unset Retention days for OpenTelemetry events and metrics SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS not passed unset Retention days for session records; 0 keeps forever CCTRACE_USERID_ACCESS_CONTROL not passed true Per-user data isolation; only false disables it STORAGE_VOLUME_PATH not passed value of WAL_DIR Path on the volume whose total, used and free space the Admin > Storage tab shows ACCESS_LOG_FILE not passed /data/logs/access.log File the HTTP access log is appended to, besides standard output; standard output only if it cannot be opened EMAIL_ALIASES not passed empty Comma-separated <alias>=<canonical> email pairs; the profile email on incoming telemetry and sync uploads is replaced by the canonical address CCTRACE_ALLOW_EMPTY_DASHBOARD not passed empty 1 starts without embedded dashboard assets

CCTRACE_AI_* variables, CODEX_API_KEY and CCTRACE_SECRETS_KEY belong to an area that is under active development and are not documented here.

docs.title: Configure the server
docs.text:
The server is configured only through environment variables. With Docker Compose you set them in the server env file (.env in the deploy/ directory), and the compose file passes a fixed subset to the cctraced container.

There are two kinds of keys:

  • Compose keys shape the containers: host ports, bind addresses, image tags, the logs directory. cctraced never sees them.
  • Server variables are read by cctraced itself. Compose passes only the ones listed in its environment: block.

deploy/.env.example is the annotated template. Run cctraced --help inside the container for the server's own list:

$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml exec cctraced cctraced --help

After changing a value, recreate the container so it takes effect:

$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

CCTRACE_AI_* variables, CODEX_API_KEY and CCTRACE_SECRETS_KEY belong to an area that is under active development and are not documented here.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Key Default Meaning JWT_SECRET none Signing key for dashboard sessions. At least 32 bytes. Compose refuses to start without it; cctraced exits on a shorter value with JWT secret must be at least 32 bytes, and on the value deploy/.env.example shipped with JWT_SECRET is a published example value. LOGS_DIR none Host directory mounted at /data/logs in the cctraced container. Compose refuses to start without it. See Operations.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning DB_PASSWORD cctrace Password of the cctrace database superuser. Applied only when the database volume is first initialised. Set it before the first start. DB_APP_CREDENTIALS empty <user>:<password> of a non-superuser role for cctraced. Set it before the first start (see below). DB_PORT 5432 Host port for TimescaleDB. Always bound to 127.0.0.1.

Compose builds DATABASE_URL for cctraced from these values. With DB_APP_CREDENTIALS empty, cctraced connects as cctrace with DB_PASSWORD.

How DB_APP_CREDENTIALS takes effect

On the first start, while the database volume is empty, deploy/initdb/10-app-role.sh creates the role named in DB_APP_CREDENTIALS as NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEROLE NOCREATEDB, and cctraced connects as that role. With the key empty, cctraced connects as the cctrace superuser, and a flaw in the server can then run commands inside the database container through COPY ... FROM PROGRAM.

The role name must not be cctrace (the superuser) or start with pg_, may contain only A-Za-z0-9_, and must be at most 63 bytes. Generate the password with only URL-safe characters, for example openssl rand -hex 20: compose writes it into the connection URL as it is, so /, #, ? or % in it leave cctraced unable to parse the URL, and that parse error contains part of the password.

docs.title: If the role was not created
docs.text:
When the value is malformed or the role cannot be created, the script prints the reason in the timescaledb log, prefixed [initdb], and skips the role; the database still finishes initialising. cctraced still connects with the credentials in DB_APP_CREDENTIALS, so it fails to authenticate until a role with that name and password exists.

Clearing DB_APP_CREDENTIALS also gets cctraced running, but as the superuser, and the tables it then creates belong to the superuser, which puts the database in the situation of the next section. As long as cctraced has never connected, the database holds none of its objects, and either of these adds the role instead:

  1. Fix the value in the server env file. Recreate the database container so it sees the new value, wait for timescaledb to show (healthy) in ps, run the script again inside it, then start the rest of the stack:

    $ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d timescaledb
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml \
    exec timescaledb sh -c 'PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" sh /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/10-app-role.sh'
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

    The script prints [initdb] created <name> (NOSUPERUSER) once the role exists.

  2. If nothing has been collected yet, remove the volumes, fix the value in the server env file, and start again. The script runs again on the empty volume.

    $ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml down -v
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

docs.title: Databases already in use
docs.text: The script runs only while the data volume is empty. On a database that is already initialised it does not run, so setting DB_APP_CREDENTIALS there points cctraced at a role that does not exist. Creating the role by hand is not enough: it must also own the objects the superuser already created, or the boot migration fails with must be owner. This repository does not include a tool for that conversion. With DB_APP_CREDENTIALS left empty, an existing deployment keeps connecting as the superuser.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning HTTP_BIND 127.0.0.1 Host address for the dashboard and REST API port GRPC_BIND 0.0.0.0 Host address for OTLP gRPC OTEL_HTTP_BIND 0.0.0.0 Host address for OTLP HTTP HTTP_PORT 8080 Host port for the dashboard and REST API GRPC_PORT 4317 Host port for OTLP gRPC OTEL_HTTP_PORT 4318 Host port for OTLP HTTP

These are compose keys. Inside the container, cctraced always listens on 8080, 4317 and 4318; the compose file sets its own HTTP_PORT, GRPC_PORT and HTTP_OTEL_PORT to those values. Note OTEL_HTTP_PORT (host, compose) versus HTTP_OTEL_PORT (container, server).

See Ports for the complete table, including the TLS overlay.

docs.title: Authentication and browser access
docs.text: Key Default Meaning CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN empty Token for creating the first admin. Empty: cctraced generates one and prints it in its log while no users exist. Invalid after the first admin is created. COOKIE_SECURE 0 1 forces the Secure flag on auth cookies. Set it when the dashboard is served over HTTPS through a proxy. Requests over TLS or with X-Forwarded-Proto: https get Secure cookies either way. CCTRACE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS empty Comma-separated browser origins on another host or port that may call the API, as exact scheme://host[:port] values without paths. No wildcard. Empty disables CORS. The bundled dashboard does not need it. API_KEY empty Optional shared API token, accepted in addition to per-user tokens. Empty disables the shared key; per-user tokens keep working.

docs.title: Sync uploads
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning CCTRACE_MAX_SYNC_BODY_BYTES 8388608 (8 MiB) Maximum size of one POST /api/sync request body. At most 268435456 (256 MiB); a larger, non-positive or non-numeric value keeps the default and logs a warning.

The client sends session records in batches and does not split a batch by size. A batch above the limit is rejected with HTTP 413, and sync of that file stops at that point. Raise the limit if your batches exceed it. The server buffers the whole body, and decoding uses roughly five times its size in memory, per request.

docs.title: Images and containers
docs.text: Key Default Meaning IMAGE_TAG latest Tag of cctrace/cctraced to run. Must match a locally built image. DB_IMAGE_TAG latest Tag of cctrace/timescaledb-pgmq to run. Must match a locally built image. CONTAINER_PREFIX cctrace Container name prefix. Change it only to run a second stack on the same host.

docs.title: Variables the compose file does not pass
docs.text:
cctraced reads the following variables, but the shipped deploy/docker-compose.yml does not list them under the cctraced service. Setting them in the server env file has no effect on the container. They apply when you run cctraced another way, or when you add them to the service's environment: yourself.

Variable Default Meaning OTEL_RETENTION_DAYS unset Retention in days for OpenTelemetry events and metrics. Unset leaves the current policy (90 days from the schema). SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS unset Retention in days for session records (conversation content). Unset leaves the current policy; 0 means keep forever. CCTRACE_USERID_ACCESS_CONTROL true Per-user isolation of session data. Only the literal value false turns it off. CCTRACE_ALLOW_EMPTY_DASHBOARD empty 1 lets cctraced start without embedded dashboard assets (API only). Without it, a binary built without the dashboard refuses to start. DATABASE_URL postgres://cctrace:cctrace@localhost:5432/cctrace?sslmode=disable Database connection string. Compose always sets it (see Database).

Retention can be set without these variables in the dashboard: Admin > Storage. See Operations.

The keys this guide covers are tabulated in Server environment. The full list of variables the server reads is what cctraced --help prints; the command is at the top of this page.

docs.title: Install the server
docs.text:
Build the two server images from this repository, write the server env file, and start the stack with Docker Compose.

The stack has two containers: cctraced (OTLP ingest, sync API, dashboard) and TimescaleDB. Both images are local build tags that no registry publishes, and the compose file sets pull_policy: never, so the stack does not start until you have built both.

Server deployment: published ports and services On the server host, docker compose runs cctraced and TimescaleDB. cctraced publishes OTLP gRPC 4317 and OTLP HTTP 4318 on all interfaces (0.0.0.0) and HTTP 8080 on loopback (127.0.0.1) by default; TimescaleDB publishes 5432 on loopback only. Claude Code sends OTLP gRPC to 4317 and Codex sends OTLP HTTP to 4318; the cctrace client uploads sessions and the browser loads the dashboard over HTTP 8080, which clients on other machines reach only after HTTP_BIND is changed or through the TLS proxy. The optional TLS overlay adds a Caddy service publishing 8443, 5317 and 5318, which proxies to cctraced over the compose network. CLIENT MACHINES SERVER HOST DOCKER COMPOSE proxy Claude Code agent Codex CLI agent cctrace session sync Browser dashboard OTLP gRPC :4317 · 0.0.0.0 OTLP HTTP :4318 · 0.0.0.0 HTTP :8080 127.0.0.1 set HTTP_BIND cctraced server TimescaleDB store 127.0.0.1:5432 Caddy optional TLS :8443 :5317 :5318

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker with the Compose plugin
  • A clone of this repository; run every command below from the repository root

docs.title: 1. Build the images
docs.text:
$ docker build -t cctrace/timescaledb-pgmq:latest docker/timescaledb-pgmq/
$ docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile --build-arg UPDATE_SIGNING=optional \
    -t cctrace/cctraced:latest .
  • The first image is TimescaleDB with the pgmq extension.
  • The second builds the dashboard and the cctraced binary inside Docker. UPDATE_SIGNING=optional builds without an update-signing key; the default, required, fails without one. Clients from an unsigned build do not update themselves. To sign the build, see Security operations.
  • If you set IMAGE_TAG or DB_IMAGE_TAG in the server env file, build with exactly that tag (cctrace/cctraced:<IMAGE_TAG>, cctrace/timescaledb-pgmq:<DB_IMAGE_TAG>). Compose does not fall back to a registry.

docs.title: 2. Write the server env file
docs.text:
Compose reads its settings from .env in the deploy/ directory (the server env file). Copy the example file, then edit the 3 keys below; every other key keeps a working default and its explanatory comment:

$ cp deploy/.env.example deploy/.env
Key Why it is required JWT_SECRET No default value worth keeping. Compose refuses to start without it, and cctraced exits if it is shorter than 32 bytes. Generate one with openssl rand -hex 32. LOGS_DIR No default. Compose refuses to start without it. Host directory mounted at /data/logs in the container. Create it in advance. DB_PASSWORD Ships with the placeholder change-me-strong-password, which you should not keep. Generate one with openssl rand -hex 20.

Edit the 3 keys in deploy/.env with your editor, or in place from the command line:

$ jwt_secret=$(openssl rand -hex 32) && sed -i.bak "s|^JWT_SECRET=.*|JWT_SECRET=${jwt_secret}|" deploy/.env
$ db_password=$(openssl rand -hex 20) && sed -i.bak "s|^DB_PASSWORD=.*|DB_PASSWORD=${db_password}|" deploy/.env
$ LOGS_DIR=/absolute/path/on/the/host/for/logs && mkdir -p "$LOGS_DIR" && sed -i.bak "s|^LOGS_DIR=.*|LOGS_DIR=${LOGS_DIR}|" deploy/.env
$ rm deploy/.env.bak

Decide DB_PASSWORD before the first start

PostgreSQL applies the password only when the data volume is initialised. Changing DB_PASSWORD afterwards leaves the database role on the old password, and cctraced restarts in a loop on password authentication failed. Recovering means removing the database volume, which deletes all collected data.

Set DB_APP_CREDENTIALS before the first start as well. With <user>:<password> there, the first start creates a non-superuser role and cctraced connects as it; left empty, cctraced connects as the database superuser. The role is created only on the first start, and its name must not be cctrace. Generate the password with openssl rand -hex 20, as for DB_PASSWORD: compose writes it into a connection URL as it is, and /, #, ? or % in it break that URL.

$ app_password=$(openssl rand -hex 20) && sed -i.bak "s|^DB_APP_CREDENTIALS=.*|DB_APP_CREDENTIALS=cctrace_app:${app_password}|" deploy/.env
$ rm deploy/.env.bak

See Configuration for the other name rules, for what to do if the first start does not create the role, and for databases already in use.

docs.title: 3. Check what the stack exposes
docs.text:
Before the first start, decide which interfaces the ports bind to.

Port Default host bind Purpose 8080 127.0.0.1 Dashboard and REST API, including client sync 4317 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) OTLP over gRPC 4318 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) OTLP over HTTP 5432 127.0.0.1 (fixed) TimescaleDB

OTLP listens on all interfaces without TLS

Ports 4317 and 4318 accept telemetry from other machines, and cctraced does not terminate TLS. On a network you do not control, set GRPC_BIND and OTEL_HTTP_BIND to a loopback or private address in the server env file, restrict the ports with a firewall or VPN, or use the HTTPS overlay.

The dashboard binds to loopback by default. For client machines to sync, they need to reach port 8080: set HTTP_BIND to a reachable address, or put a TLS-terminating proxy in front of it. The full port table is in Ports.

docs.title: 4. Start the stack
docs.text:
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

up -d returning cleanly means the containers were created, not that the server started. cctraced reports configuration errors in its own log.

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml ps
$ curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/health
  • Both containers should show Up with (healthy). The cctraced health check probes /api/version and has a 30-second start period, so it shows health: starting at first.
  • /api/health answers with "status":"ok" when the server can reach the database, and with HTTP 503 and "status":"unhealthy" when it cannot.
  • If cctraced is Restarting, read its log:
$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml logs cctraced

docs.title: 6. Create the first admin
docs.text:
On a database with no users, cctraced prints a one-time setup token in its log:

[cctraced] initial administrator setup token: <token>

To choose the token yourself, set CCTRACE_SETUP_TOKEN in the server env file before the first start. The token stops working once the first admin exists. Continue with First admin.

docs.title: Optional: HTTPS with Caddy
docs.text:
deploy/docker-compose.tls.yml is an opt-in overlay that adds a Caddy container. Caddy terminates TLS for all three listeners and forwards to cctraced over the compose network, using deploy/caddy/Caddyfile. The base compose file is unchanged, and Caddy's image (caddy:2-alpine) is pulled from Docker Hub.

  1. In the server env file, move the plaintext ports to loopback and name the server:

    HTTP_BIND=127.0.0.1
GRPC_BIND=127.0.0.1
OTEL_HTTP_BIND=127.0.0.1
CADDY_SITE_ADDRESS=cctrace.company.example

    CADDY_SITE_ADDRESS is required by the overlay. It can be a hostname or the server's IP address. Without the three bind settings, the plaintext ports stay reachable beside the TLS ones.

  2. Start with both compose files:

    $ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env \
    -f deploy/docker-compose.yml -f deploy/docker-compose.tls.yml up -d
Channel Plaintext (container) TLS (host default) Dashboard and REST API 8080 8443 OTLP gRPC 4317 5317 OTLP HTTP 4318 5318

Clients then use https://cctrace.company.example:8443 for the dashboard and sync, and port 5317 or 5318 for OTLP.

Codex sends OTLP/HTTP, so cctrace derives its metrics endpoint from the profile's OTEL endpoint by changing port 5317 to 5318, as it changes 4317 to 4318. With an internal CA, Codex also needs that CA in its configuration; see below and Codex CLI.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
CADDY_TLS_MODE defaults to internal: Caddy issues certificates from its own CA, which needs no public DNS and works for a bare IP address. Clients must trust that CA. Export it with:

$ docker compose --env-file deploy/.env \
    -f deploy/docker-compose.yml -f deploy/docker-compose.tls.yml \
    exec caddy cat /data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt > cctrace-ca.crt

Copy the file to each client machine and give it to cctrace once. cctrace init asks for it when an endpoint is https://, or set it directly:

$ cctrace config set server.ca_cert_file ~/cctrace-ca.crt

Give it even if the CA is already in the OS keychain; whether the keychain alone is enough for Claude Code and Codex was not tested. Each client takes its CA from a different place, and cctrace writes the one file to each:

Client Where it reads the CA Who sets it cctrace system roots plus server.ca_cert_file cctrace Claude Code NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS in its settings file, with the exporter on http/protobuf to 5318 (why) cctrace Codex tls = { ca-certificate = "..." } in its [otel] section cctrace

A running sync daemon keeps the CA it started with; restart it after setting or clearing the CA (cctrace sync --stop, then start it as usual). Codex's section is rewritten when sync next starts. See Set up the client.

The initial curl download of the client binary does not use this setting; add --cacert cctrace-ca.crt to it. See Install the client.

Set CADDY_TLS_MODE to an ACME account email address (for example ops@example.com) when the name resolves publicly and port 80 is reachable from the internet — the word acme itself makes Caddy refuse to start. Caddy then obtains a publicly trusted certificate, and cctrace and Claude Code need no CA configuration. Codex against a public certificate without server.ca_cert_file was not measured.

Keep the caddy_data volume

It holds the issued certificates and the internal CA. Removing it creates a new CA, and every client that trusted the old one stops connecting.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
